A Save the Children report released Thursday found that 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones in 2025, a record high since records began in 1990 and more than double the total from the mid-1990s. Florian Westphal, CEO of Save the Children Germany, described the situation as requiring a wake-up call for the international community.

Geographically, around two in five children lived in conflict zones across both Africa and the Middle East in 2025. Africa alone accounted for 44% of all such children worldwide. In the Middle East, 40.2% of children were affected, a figure that rose nearly 29%, from 52 million in 2024 to 67 million in 2025. Across Africa, exposure has more than tripled over the past 15 years, with the share rising from 12% in 2010 to 39% in 2025.

The report highlighted a dramatic increase in the denial of humanitarian access, recording 8,322 verified incidents in 2025. This represents a 16-fold rise over the past decade; the figure was 509 in 2015 and only eight when the UN established its Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in 2005. The Palestinian Territories accounted for the vast majority of cases, with 5,946 incidents or more than 70% of all verified cases globally. Denial of humanitarian access rose from around 2% of all verified grave violations against children in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, becoming the second-most frequently recorded violation after killing and maiming.

Overall, the UN verified 38,967 grave violations against children in 2025. This was the second-highest annual total since the MRM's establishment, surpassed only by the record 41,763 documented in 2024. More than half of these occurred in three areas: the Palestinian Territories, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and Nigeria. The Palestinian Territories alone accounted for 12,449 verified violations, nearly one-third of all cases.

Beyond denial of humanitarian access, other recorded violations included 14,224 children killed or maimed in conflicts; a record 5,128 child abductions; 1,787 cases of sexual violence, up 71% over the past decade; and 2,930 attacks on schools and hospitals, marking a fifth straight year of increases. The Palestinian Territories recorded the most attacks on schools or hospitals with 837 incidents, followed by Ukraine with 643; together these two accounted for more than half of all reported cases worldwide. Sexual violence saw its sharpest rises in the DRC, where cases jumped from 358 in 2024 to 592 in 2025, and Sudan, which rose from 74 to 193; around 86% of sexual violence cases were documented in African conflict zones. Save the Children concluded that changing these odds requires political choices prioritizing children's safety.
items.title: Save the Children: Record Number of Children Living in Conflict Zones

items.summary: The Senate was set to vote on amendments and final passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting reform bill that only requires a bare majority. The article notes it had survived the 60-vote cloture threshold through procedural votes rather than constitutional requirements. Nearly every Republican voted in favor across cloture votes, with Mike Rounds being the sole senator to vote no on all roll calls, while Josh Hawley switched from yes to no after opposing transmission provisions. Democratic support eroded over time: fourteen Democrats never voted against the bill, but 25 opposed it at each opportunity, including Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Ed Markey, and Ron Wyden. Some senators who initially supported cloture later peeled off on final votes, notably Jon Ossoff, Gary Peters, Jeanne Shaheen, Cathy Cortez Masto, Richard Blumenthal, and Andy Kim. The article highlighted same-state splits within the Democratic caucus, such as Raphael Warnock voting yes while Jon Ossoff switched to no in Georgia; Martin Heinrich supporting versus Ben Ray Lujan opposing in New Mexico; Mark Kelly against but Ruben Gallego for in Arizona; and Cory Booker for while Andy Kim flipped from yes to no in New Jersey. A divide emerged between a self-described "new school" climate hawk, Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, signaling he would vote yes on final passage, versus the older generation including Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse who argued the bill benefits the climate by speeding permitting and leveling clean energy with fossil fuels; yet even aggressive advocates like Tina Smith opposed it over concerns for mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The article then turned to the National Historic Preservation Act section of BAAJA, which critics say impinges on tribal sovereignty through a revised Section 106 review process featuring fewer dialogue opportunities and stricter deadlines: agencies would have just 30 days for stakeholders to respond before consultation begins in theory, with tribes having only 45 days to object or risk the agency proceeding without their participation. Wesley Furlong of the Native American Rights Fund argued soliciting information rather than genuine consultation is an affront to tribal nations, while Ira Matt of the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Offices called changes made without tribe involvement unacceptable and likened earlier provisions echoing termination-era policies to a shift toward assimilation-era tactics. The bill authorizes $200 million per year for state and tribal preservation offices, though Furlong noted this is not an appropriation commitment since Congress must still fund the Historic Preservation Fund annually. BAAJA also bars courts from issuing injunctions or vacating permits when agencies fail to follow law, a change some legal scholars argue renders both NHPA and NEPA toothless by removing litigation incentives; David Tatel of the D.C. Circuit wrote that without meaningful court relief there would be little constraint on agencies. An amendment proposed by California Senator Alex Padilla sought to exempt tribal government claims from this judicial review limit, though it raised questions about consistency with non-tribal claims. Proponents countered that Trump administration regulatory changes strip consultation more explicitly and that BAAJA enshrines protection in permanent law, a point Furlong disputed given only regulations could be challenged or changed by future administrations. Negotiations were conducted behind closed doors without hearings, committee markups, or reports typical of the process, prompting an October 23 letter from indigenous-led nonprofits calling tribal exclusion unacceptable; however, some groups like the National Tribal Energy Association and Apsáalooke Nation/Crow Tribe supported the bill while the Coalition of Large Tribes submitted redlines. The Murkowski-Schatz amendment filed Tuesday would make a small change ensuring federally funded projects undergo NHPA reviews rather than only those requiring federal approval, though its text was reportedly still in flux. The most recent procedural vote saw 70 senators agree to advance the bill, with many advocating for NHPA changes such as Cortez-Masto, Schiff, Padilla, and Mark Kelly not among them, suggesting tribal concerns may not threaten passage.
items.title: Senate Votes on Bipartisan Permitting Bill Amid Tribal Sovereignty Debate

The article explains how the 2026 Australian Football League (AFL) draft works as all 18 clubs prepare for selection day. The draft runs across two nights on November 19 and November 20, with first-round prospects named on night one before later rounds proceed on the following evening. Both nights begin at 7pm AEDT, with corresponding times listed for South Australia (6:30pm ACDT), Queensland (6pm AEST), Northern Territory (5:30pm ACST) and Western Australia (4pm AWST). ABC Sport will run live blogs on both nights, while Fox Footy and Kayo Sports carry the broadcast. The piece notes that academies and father-son selections have complicated the process for clubs seeking top talent.

Regarding early picks, Dougie Cochrane is tied to Port Adelaide through its Next Generation Academy (NGA), while Cody Walker is bound to Carlton under the father-son rule after his father Andrew played 202 games for the club. In the open pool, Ethan Drever is expected to be selected by Essendon once Port's bid on Cochrane is matched at the top of the draft. The article suggests Richmond will face an interesting decision when selecting behind Essendon, with Arki Butler, Harry Van Hattum and Heath Mellody all in consideration.

The first-round pick order listed runs: Essendon; Richmond; West Coast; Melbourne (received from Port Adelaide via trade); Richmond (received from Port Adelaide via trade); Sydney (received from North Melbourne via trade); Port Adelaide (received from Melbourne via trade); Gold Coast (free agency compensation pick); GWS Giants; St Kilda; Collingwood; Port Adelaide (received from Melbourne via trade); Carlton; Melbourne (received from Western Bulldogs via trade); Adelaide; St Kilda (received from Geelong via trade); Essendon (received from Hawthorn via trade); Carlton (received from Sydney via 2025 Curnow trade); Fremantle; and GWS Giants (received from Brisbane via trade).

The bidding system assigns each pick a points value, with the first pick worth 3,000 points decreasing to 14 points at pick 54 in the third round. Picks beyond that carry no points value. Several changes this year make it harder for higher-placed clubs to match bids on academy prospects: clubs can now use only two picks to match a bid up to and including pick 36; discounts or loadings apply based on ladder position; previous grand finalists must pay 20 per cent extra while preliminary final teams pay 10 per cent extra; clubs finishing between fifth and tenth receive no discount or loading, while those outside the top 10 get a 10 per cent discount; and bottom-five clubs whose first pick is pushed back by a matched bid are compensated with an extra second-round pick.

Draft-day trades have been permitted since their introduction in 2018. Teams may trade using picks from the current draft as well as picks from the 2027 or 2028 drafts. The article closes with first-pick selections over the last decade: Willem Duursma (West Coast, 2025), Sam Lalor (Richmond, 2024), Harley Reid (West Coast, 2023), Aaron Cadman (GWS Giants, 2022), Jason Horne-Francis (North Melbourne, 2021), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan (Western Bulldogs, 2020), Matt Rowell (Gold Coast, 2019), Sam Walsh (Carlton, 2018), Cam Rayner (Brisbane, 2017) and Andrew McGrath (Essendon, 2016).
items.title: Guide to the 2026 AFL draft dates, rules and top picks

items.summary: Finshots examines Mahanadi Coalfields Limited's (MCL) initial public offering, framed as a window into coal's future in India amid rapidly growing electricity demand from new homes, electric vehicles, expanding industries, and data centres. Despite ambitious renewable energy targets, coal supplied close to 45% of the country's installed capacity as of 2025, keeping it central to power generation because solar and wind cannot always guarantee dependable supply. MCL, a subsidiary of Coal India operating in Odisha's Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields, is India's largest coal producer by volume; in FY26 it produced around 218 million tonnes, roughly 21% of domestic output, supplying thermal power plants as well as aluminium, cement, and sponge iron industries. The listing takes the form of a 100% offer for sale (OFS) by its promoter Coal India Ltd., which is offering up to 661.84 million equity shares at a price band of ₹129-136 per share; because it is entirely an OFS, MCL itself receives no money and the proceeds go to Coal India as part of its broader plan to unlock value from subsidiaries, having already taken Bharat Coking Coal Limited public in January 2026 and Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Limited in March 2026. A key concern for investors is pricing power: most coal sells through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) at base prices notified centrally by Coal India, with MCL primarily supplying utility-grade non-coking coal, grades G11 to G14; FSAs accounted for around 82.12% of product sales in FY26 at an average realisation of approximately ₹1,354 per tonne, while the remaining 17.88% sold through electronic auctions fetched about ₹1,797 per tonne, with e-auctions allowing MCL to earn a premium over notified prices that can materially affect profitability given its scale. Between FY24 and FY26, dispatches reached a record 210.74 million tonnes in FY26 yet revenue fell from ₹31,634 crore to ₹30,550 crore because auction premiums normalised: the premium dropped from around ₹802 per tonne above notified prices in FY24 to approximately ₹275 per tonne by FY26. Even so, MCL remains highly profitable with an EBITDA margin of 47.45% and a PAT margin of 31.56%, generating over ₹10,698 crore in profits against debt of just ₹3.16 crore as of March 2026. Logistics matter for such volumes: rail accounted for 65.28% of dispatches in FY26, up from 58.70% in FY24 while road fell to 30.74%, and the company is investing in First-Mile Connectivity infrastructure like silos and rapid-loading systems, with over 96% of dispatches through this infrastructure rail-based; it also has access to five seaports handling around 21.5% of dispatches to supply coastal power plants that might otherwise rely on imported coal. Risks include customer concentration, since the top 10 customers accounted for 55.94% of revenue in FY26 and a few large buyers reducing purchases or switching suppliers could affect MCL; competition from private commercial mines encouraged by reforms and captive blocks developed by industrial buyers that may reduce demand over time; and the energy transition as renewable capacity expands, which could gradually change coal-fired power economics even though reserves are vast. The article concludes that while MCL has enormous reserves to sustain production for decades with further resource conversion extending that horizon, the real question is whether India will keep needing coal at scale and whether MCL can maintain its exceptional economics as the energy mix shifts away from coal.
items.title: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO Explained

items.summary: Housing minister Matthew Pennycook is introducing a government leasehold reform bill that will cap annual ground rent at £250 for leaseholders in England and Wales, with enforcement expected around 2028 rather than sooner. He described the measure as marking 'the beginning of the end for the feudal leasehold system,' which he characterises as an anachronism dating back to feudal property laws that exists in only a few countries worldwide. The bill will also extend the ban on new leasehold properties from houses to flats, making it the biggest step toward ending the system; Pennycook expects this ban to come into force after the next election. Additional provisions include easing the switch to commonhold by requiring agreement from half of residents rather than all of them in a block, and ending freeholders' right to evict leaseholders over small unpaid bills. MPs on the housing select committee had urged introduction as soon as next year, but Pennycook said enforcement could not begin that quickly due to the 'technical process,' with the 2028 date set through secondary legislation rather than explicitly in the bill. Other demands, such as an independent regulator for property management agents and changes to lease extension costs, would require a second law later in parliament, while ministers still consider proposals to remove future development costs from lease prices. Pennycook attributed delays to the complexity of drafting the legislation, calling it 'by far and away the most complex and technical piece of legislation I have ever dealt with' and warning that vested interests with deep pockets will almost certainly challenge it, as occurred with the 2024 Act.
items.title: England and Wales leasehold reform bill caps ground rent in 2028

items.summary: Elderly women have camped for 12 days near the Meghalaya state secretariat in Shillong, demanding that a proposed ropeway be scrapped. Announced in December 2024, the project would run nearly one kilometre of cable cars to Shillong Peak and cost Rs 175 crore; the government claims it will generate at least Rs 10 crore annually while creating jobs and business for locals. Residents opposing it are organized as the Joint Action Committee Against the Shillong Ropeway Project, formed by Laban Pyllun residents who argue the project endangers streams in Lum Shyllong, a forested hill considered sacred in Khasi mythology as home to Lei Shyllong, the deity of nine river sources. Deborah Marbaniang, head of the committee, told Scroll that all drinking water for the city comes from this area and said felling over 544 mature trees is already affecting supply, with at least 2,000 more expected; poet Janice Pariat questioned how many trees lie in the 2.3 hectares cleared and warned of disruption to landing platforms and posts up to 40 metres high in a seismic zone. The government denies any risk: Deputy Chief Minister Prestone Tynsong said it would not scrap or relocate the project on "unfounded fears," while CVD Diengdoh, CEO of the Meghalaya Ropeway Development Authority, met with committee members and asserted that six towers occupying 0.2 per cent of the catchment area would leave spring sources unaffected because the ropeway passes above the tree line to minimize felling. Officials also said all mandatory approvals were secured before work began in October, including clearance from the Union Ministry of Environment for diverting 2.32 hectares and a lease from Riat Laban Dorbar Pyllun; they cited a public consultation held in September 2022 with representatives present, though Marbaniang called it a sham. The dispute has also drawn KHADC into conflict with the ruling National People's Party government: run by the Voice of People's Party opposition and empowered under the Sixth Schedule to regulate trading licences for non-tribal players, the council alleged that contractors KEC International Ltd and Tantia Construction Ltd failed to obtain a mandatory licence. On October 27, Denzil R Chen, an executive member of the council, said heavy machinery was stopped before permissions were secured; the gates at the Lawsohtun lower terminal site were locked two days later, prompting the government to lodge a first information report against an inspector for sealing it. Experts note the absence of a rigorous environmental audit: Professor Devesh Walia of North-Eastern Hill University said that if the ropeway runs above the tree line it should cause little damage and urged scientific evidence over emotional appeals, while attributing dried springs possibly to variable rainfall rather than the project; he called for an independent study with disclosed findings. A minister proposed an expert panel from Indian Institutes of Technology, which the committee rejected in favor of scrapping the project entirely. One activist claimed residents are divided, with half supporting it and dismissing objections as emotional appeals by those without technical expertise who simply want to keep tourism out of their backyard; Marbaniang countered that the threat extends beyond Laban to a 15-km stretch of green cover across the city.
items.title: Protesters and officials clash over a Shillong ropeway

items.summary: Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council (USCBC), frames the business community as more than an economic player at APEC, describing it instead as a force for change. He highlights APEC's role in bringing governments and businesses together to share best practices, push for policy improvements, and turn innovation into real-world solutions. Stein notes that governments create the conditions for growth while businesses drive innovation, arguing that real progress occurs when these two sectors work together.
items.title: US-China Business Council President on APEC's Role in Government-Business Collaboration

items.summary: An opinion piece argues that Australia, already described by The New York Times in 2019 as 'the world's most secretive democracy', faces worsening transparency problems through a defence capabilities and protecting bases bill being rushed through parliament. The author contends that successive defence, anti-terror and surveillance bills across consecutive governments have shifted power from the legislature to the executive. Under the proposed legislation, the minister could grant exemptions from Australian laws to defence officials, with the definition of 'defence official' expanded to include third-party contractors working for the Department of Defence. The author warns this would permit private military contractors operating as mercenaries in Australia to act without legal accountability. The piece links this development to tech corporations expanding into national defence work, naming OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft and Palantir as companies now serving defence departments while operating on civilian internet infrastructure. It cites a recent government announcement that OpenAI would not face criminal charges over a Medicare data breach, characterizing the move as the government accepting corporate misconduct in pursuit of productivity gains. The author argues the bill would give the defence minister discretion to designate staff at these corporations as 'defence officials' with pre-emptive legal exemptions, subject only to national security provisions that limit public and parliamentary scrutiny while imposing heavy penalties on whistleblowers. The article also discusses 'defence security zones,' which allow the minister to classify both military and civilian infrastructure for restricted access; it references Pine Gap as an existing example where Australians cannot enter or photograph the site. Extending this concept, the author claims AI corporations building datacentres in suburban areas would be protected from local opposition, with protests against these facilities potentially criminalized under the bill's designation powers. The piece concludes by framing Australia's lack of a human rights act as an urgent problem and calling for stronger legal protections for civilians rather than expanded dispensations to corporate actors.
items.title: Australia's proposed defence exemptions bill raises secrecy concerns

items.summary: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has proposed a revised aircraft registration framework that would create a separate mechanism for prototype and production test flights, allowing manufacturers to obtain dedicated registration marks without entering the aircraft in India's regular civil register. Under this proposal, applicants must apply through the DGCA's e-GCA portal using a distinct form and submit production approval documents such as a letter of agreement from the Aircraft Engineering Directorate or a production organisation approval from the DGCA or a foreign authority. Registration fees would be calculated based on an aircraft's maximum take-off weight (MTOW) as specified in its type certificate data sheet, and the marks would be reserved exclusively for test flights with no other permitted use. The draft specifies that these certificates expire once the manufacturer issues a statement of design conformity (Form CA-52), after which holders must obtain a certificate of non-registration before reusing the mark on another aircraft; the expired registration mark and the aircraft's 24-bit Mode-S code would also have to be removed. Separately, applications for dry lease registrations would require copies of the lease agreement plus an original 'no binding certificate' from the owner, lessor, lessee and mortgagee stating that no clause binds the regulator, while once entered in the Indian Civil Aircraft Register a registration mark cannot be reallocated. The revisions align with broader government efforts to strengthen India's aircraft leasing and financing ecosystem following Parliament's passage of the Protection of Interest in Aircraft Objects Bill, 2025, which aims to bring the framework closer to the Cape Town Convention; although India acceded to that convention in 2008, civil aviation ministry figures indicate enforcement gaps have kept leasing costs 8-10% higher than elsewhere. The DGCA has invited public comments before finalising the changes.
items.title: DGCA Proposes Separate Registration System for Prototype and Production Aircraft

items.summary: The China Manned Space Agency says the Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship will be launched at an appropriate time in the near future. The combination of the spaceship and its Long March-2F carrier rocket was moved to the launch area on Tuesday at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, where additional work is scheduled over the coming days to ensure a safe and smooth mission. People who attended the transfer witnessed the move and sent their best wishes for the flight.
items.title: Shenzhou-24 spacecraft transferred ahead of launch

items.summary: Speaking at Columbia University in New York, Rahul Gandhi, Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, warned that India faces an economic disaster marked by massive unemployment and a failing education system. He blamed the Union government for these conditions and argued that its flagship initiatives—Make in India and Startup India—had produced no results because "the spine of the economy has been broken." Gandhi compared India's model to China's, noting that while China had succeeded at manufacturing blue-collar jobs, two businessmen controlling a country's economic architecture could not sustain production. He framed global street protests as symptoms of shared socioeconomic frustration across nations and suggested India's lower costs and larger population made it better positioned than the US or Germany to provide youth employment despite greater hardship. Gandhi also reiterated allegations of electoral malpractice and his party's push to remove election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, warning that a government response could turn "violently and aggressively." His remarks drew sharp criticism from BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia, who accused Gandhi of making false statements abroad designed to undermine India's progress and international image. The speech was the first of two planned US engagements for Gandhi, with his next appearance set at the University of Chicago on Thursday.
items.title: Rahul Gandhi warns of economic crisis at Columbia University; BJP rebuts

items.summary: The sitting leaders of the United States, China and Russia are set to hold a landmark trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday (November 19), marking their first face-to-face meeting as heads of state. The talks will open at 2.30 pm local time (12 noon IST) on the sidelines of the APEC summit, preceded by a brief bilateral between Trump and Xi Jinping, and are expected to last no more than an hour according to the Kremlin; the leaders had already met informally at a welcome banquet hosted by Xi on Wednesday evening. The agenda is understood to centre on global security, strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction, with particular attention given to reviving arms-control talks after the New START treaty between Washington and Moscow expired in February 2026. Trump has pushed for China's inclusion in future frameworks alongside Russia, though Beijing has shown limited enthusiasm for formal limits on its arsenal; analysts note that China is estimated to hold more than 600 nuclear warheads compared with over 5,000 each for the US and Russia. The leaders are also expected to discuss artificial intelligence risks in military decision-making, including proposals for human oversight of nuclear launch systems, as well as major conflicts such as the Russia-Ukraine war and the conflict involving Iran; Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov has said Ukraine is on the agenda while noting that the summit's schedule remains fluid. Trump will also hold one-on-one talks with Putin, their first direct meeting since last year's Alaska discussions failed to end the war in Kyiv's favour. Elon Musk accompanies the US delegation, drawing attention because SpaceX's Starshield satellite system has supported Ukrainian drone missions and communications during the conflict. For India, observers are watching for signals on how power is shifting among three countries central to New Delhi's foreign policy; analysts note that while Trump emphasises personal diplomacy, the Xi-Putin strategic partnership remains considerably deeper than either leader's ties with Washington.
items.title: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen

items.summary:
At a fireside chat with New York Times columnist Lydia Polgreen at Columbia University, Rahul Gandhi addressed an audience of students and faculty while directing his remarks toward India. He arrived in New York on Tuesday morning (November 17), and the conversation was uploaded to public platforms Wednesday evening after including student questions.

On democracy, Gandhi argued that India's crisis extends beyond elections because a concentration of political and economic power has weakened ordinary people's ability to be heard. He pointed to protests by Adivasis, Dalits, and farmers as resistance against this concentration over nearly a decade, stating there is "a massive concentration of wealth taking place in India and huge disenfranchisement of people." Regarding democratic institutions, he said participation becomes difficult when those institutions cannot function independently, and he reiterated his demand for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. On student protests, Gandhi noted that people were no longer afraid to express themselves after years of fearing action from investigative agencies or police.

Unemployment dominated the hour-long conversation as India's economic model failed to deliver results for educated youth. Gandhi argued the problem was not opportunities abroad but a domestic economy unable to create enough jobs, saying "The crux of it is that they do not see a future for themselves." He stressed that education alone does not guarantee employment and recalled meeting an engineer working as a coolie at Delhi railway station. He questioned the BJP-led Centre's Make in India and Startup India initiatives over unfulfilled job and manufacturing promises, and cited demonetisation, GST implementation, and Covid-19 disruptions as factors hurting small businesses.

On political ideology, Gandhi rejected Western left-right frameworks, stating "There is no left and right in India. Left and right is a Western concept." He framed the contest between Congress and BJP as two competing visions of the country that have each existed for thousands of years, with Congress's philosophy rooted in protecting every individual's expression regardless of background.

On China, Gandhi used its manufacturing dominance to highlight what he believes India gets wrong economically. He noted China controls large parts of global production and is moving toward new technologies like electric mobility, but also criticized the political system as undemocratic and brutal. He said he was not interested in replicating it but wanted India to learn from its emphasis on production while retaining democracy.

On his Bharat Jodo Yatra, Gandhi described how the 4,000-kilometre walk transformed his understanding of Indian politics after Congress began questioning the electoral system's functioning. He called it "the most beautiful experience of my life" and said conventional politics assumes leaders know what is best for people, whereas he argued that listening to people is the only real political model.

Gandhi concluded by returning to India's future, arguing the country must restore democratic participation while building an economy capable of providing opportunities. He framed his entire address around one argument: India's future depends on giving ordinary people a greater say in how the country is governed and how its wealth and opportunities are created.
items.title: Rahul Gandhi's Columbia University Address: Five Key Points

items.summary: Crude oil production in the Permian basin, which spans Texas and New Mexico, has remained moderate even as a war premium pushed prices above $100 per barrel. The Permian has driven U.S. crude output growth for over a decade, with annual gains consistently exceeding 1 million barrels until pandemic lockdowns in 2020 briefly drove prices negative. Since then, both shale and Permian production growth have slowed. The basin still accounts for about 45% of the national total and remains the largest contributor to overall U.S. crude output growth. Enverus expects total U.S. crude oil production to rise by 378,000 barrels daily this year, with most coming from the Permian; Bloomberg noted that would represent a 2.8% annual increase versus 1.6% for 2025 over 2024. Enverus analyst Stephen Sagriff said many operators are adding small amounts of drilling that aggregate into significant change. According to the Energy Information Administration, Permian production averaged 6.84 million barrels daily in the third quarter, up slightly from 6.82 million in the second quarter, with an expected rise to 6.91 million for the current quarter and a forecast exceeding 7 million barrels daily by 2027, up from just 2.2 million in 2017. Some analysts warn that fast Permian growth carries rising costs as horizontal wells lengthen and fracking fluid demand grows, with wastewater storage capacity running low last year and regulators expected to limit new disposal licenses. Others argue ample oil remains to support U.S. output for years or decades; Slav concludes the latter view is correct given slower but natural price-responsive growth. Amid a squeeze from war between the United States and Israel against Iran, Diamondback announced this week it would buy $5 billion in assets from Double Eagle, part of recent Permian-focused consolidation after megadeals shrank the pool of large targets. Forecasters do not expect a return to original boom-year rates; most project steady growth peaking at around 7.7 million barrels daily near 2035, followed by a plateau rather than a sharp decline that could offset natural declines elsewhere in the United States.
items.title: Permian crude output growth moderates despite war-driven price surge

items.summary: Greenpeace activists dropped several large boulders on the seafloor of the U.K.'s Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area, a nearly 37,000 square kilometer (about 14,000 square miles) zone that is part of the country's network contributing to its goal of protecting 30% of Earth's land and sea by 2030. Despite this designation, bottom trawl fishing remains permitted in the area; a practice using weighted nets dragged along the seabed. Greenpeace U.K.'s head of oceans, Elena Polisano, described the protected zone as little more than a paper park, calling it false advertising because marine life is not actually safeguarded there. She said the fishers bulldoze the seabed and pulverize marine life while killing porpoises, sharks, dolphins, seabirds, and other species. To create obstacles for bottom trawlers, Greenpeace placed 10 boulders on the seafloor, each weighing about 2 tonnes (4,400 pounds). One was carved in the likeness of naturalist David Attenborough and nicknamed "Attenboulder." Polisano told Mongabay that the rocks will not necessarily stop bottom trawlers but will create new obstacles for their operations. The European Bottom Fisheries Alliance condemned Greenpeace's actions, arguing environmental protection cannot be achieved by bypassing regulations and unilaterally imposing fishing restrictions, and warning that publishing coordinates afterward does not eliminate danger to fishers' lives. The U.K.'s Marine Management Organisation said it is investigating the group but declined further comment on the ongoing inquiry. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs stated in an email to Mongabay that strict legislation protects the marine environment while supporting sustainable fishing, adding that activities at sea should be carried out lawfully with due regard for other users' safety. Greenpeace has used this tactic before; in 2020 and 2021 it deployed similar boulders in the Dogger Bank MPA and Offshore Brighton MPA. A judge ruled the MMO had jurisdiction but asked it to reconsider whether prosecution served the public interest, after which the MMO dropped the case. Months later a government byelaw banning bottom towed fishing gear across the Dogger Bank Special Area of Conservation came into force. Polisano said Greenpeace cannot do all of government's job and urged officials to act on their commitments before time runs out.
items.title: Greenpeace deploys Attenboulder boulders to deter bottom trawlers in UK marine protected area

items.summary: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" over the record amount he spent backing Republicans in the US midterms, following sweeping Democratic victories. As the election's top individual donor, Musk gave $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, with much of the spending concentrated in Texas, where many of his companies are based. Speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference for business and political leaders, Musk also said he was "not Maga," describing it as blind adherence to a set of Republican policies that he did not share. The midterms were seen as a bruising defeat for Trump amid pressure over his impact on US living costs, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress after flipping swing seats and making historic gains in long-standing Republican areas. Musk acknowledged the heavy losses could affect him and his businesses: incoming Democratic majorities have pledged greater scrutiny of tech firms, including over controversial data centres, while a newly elected Democrat governor in Georgia promised to limit their rollout and associated tax breaks. Lawmakers also suggested SpaceX should be investigated after gaining an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump's re-election. Musk conceded he did not see much return from the spending but added that candidates would likely have fared worse without it. The results are significant for Texas specifically, where Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat after Musk had reportedly spent at least $45m supporting him; SpaceX operates data centres there too. Musk characterized Texas's new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated three-decade-long Republican control by beating Governor Greg Abbott, as "quite moderate," adding that he did not think she was far-left and expected things to be fine in the state under her leadership.
items.title: Musk regrets record midterm spending after Republican defeats

items.summary: The United States and China, described as the world's two largest economies, have agreed to build a constructive strategic stability relationship grounded in respect, fairness, and reciprocity, with cooperation as its main theme. The article frames trade as one of the most measurable forms of that cooperation. According to figures presented for the period from 2001 to 2025, US goods exports to China grew by 454.2%, a figure more than double the 198.6% growth in US exports to the rest of the world over the same span. In 2025, China ranked as the largest export market for US soybeans, the second-largest for integrated circuits, and the third-largest for medical devices. The article also notes that the United States was the largest contributor to China's services trade deficit. These figures are presented by the source as reflecting the mutually beneficial nature of economic ties between the two countries.
items.title: US-China Trade Figures Highlight Economic Interdependence

items.summary:
Anthropic PBC is set to become the first frontier AI lab to go public, debuting Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. The company priced its shares at $83 each on Wednesday, giving it a roughly $1.5 trillion valuation, about $100 billion above the high end of its previous range. Bloomberg estimates indicate that several financial firms stand to gain billions from the offering.

Iconiq funneled more than $6 billion into Anthropic and holds the largest private investment in its history; based on pre-IPO investments, its stake would be worth over $26 billion at the IPO valuation. Spark Capital invested $75 million in 2023, marking its largest check ever, with a current stake valued at about $11 billion. Menlo Ventures led Anthropic's Series D round with a $500 million check and has invested north of $1 billion total, holding a stake worth nearly $22 billion.

Guy Oseary and Ashton Kutcher wrote an early $35 million check before adding another $400 million; together with Sound Ventures' Effie Epstein, they hold a stake worth nearly $11 billion. Coatue Management invested three times for a total of $4.75 billion, including $2.5 billion in the February round as its largest single private company investment at the time, yielding a stake valued at about $16 billion. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC has invested north of $4.5 billion across Anthropic's last three rounds and holds a stake worth about $15 billion.

Bessemer Venture Partners invested over $800 million for around 0.5% ownership, or about $7.5 billion at the IPO price, representing more than ninefold growth from its initial investment. Lightspeed put more than $3.5 billion into Anthropic starting in early 2024 and planned further IPO investment; based on private financings alone, its stake is valued at about $28 billion. General Catalyst backed Anthropic across various rounds starting in 2025 with approximately $2 billion, holding a stake worth around $10 billion.

Anthropic's largest stakeholders are by far its Big Tech backers: Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc.'s Google, and Microsoft Corp. all hold stakes worth tens of billions after years of investing and partnering with the lab. Anthropic also arranged a $26 billion private placement for seven tech companies to invest further; after those transactions, Amazon owns nearly 15% of Anthropic's outstanding stock and Google owns about 14%. These four companies have been criticized for creating circular deals in which they are simultaneously investors, customers, and distributors while selling competing AI models. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt invested tens of millions in the company in 2021 when it was valued at just $461 million; at a $1.5 trillion IPO price, his stake is expected to be worth about $15 billion.

The reporting relies on Bloomberg estimates and information from people familiar with details who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Calculations may not account for dilution from the IPO, allocations in pending orders are undisclosed, and all parties either declined or did not respond to comment requests.
items.title: Financial investors' windfalls from Anthropic's record IPO

items.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday that China and the Republic of Korea (ROK) have substantially concluded the second phase of negotiations on their Free Trade Agreement. A ministry official stated in response to a media query that this outcome will create new opportunities for enterprises in both countries, consolidate the foundation of bilateral economic and trade cooperation, and inject fresh impetus into the steady development of the China-ROK strategic cooperative partnership. The official also framed the achievement as a pragmatic measure by both sides to uphold multilateralism and free trade while opposing unilateralism and protectionism and safeguarding the multilateral trading system. The second phase upgraded the investment, trade in services, financial services, and economic cooperation chapters along with related annexes of the original agreement. Officials noted these upgrades will expand and improve China-ROK investment and trade in services, strengthen bilateral economic and trade relations, and achieve higher-level mutually beneficial outcomes. Based on this substantial conclusion, both sides are preparing for the formal signing of the upgraded agreement. The FTA was originally signed on June 1, 2015, and entered into force on December 20, 2015. According to China's official statistics, China-ROK trade reached $331.24 billion in 2025, with bilateral trade standing at $440.9 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surging by 63.7% year on year.
items.title: China-ROK FTA Second Phase Negotiations Concluded

items.summary: Nvidia delivered strong third-quarter results on Tuesday, posting bumper revenue and earnings alongside sales projections that beat Wall Street estimates. Its shares rose as much as 5% in extended trading. This rebound comes after the company's share price fell nearly 40% from its October 6 record high, wiping roughly $2 trillion off its market capitalization and ending its status as the world's most valuable company. The bulk of that decline occurred before Jensen Huang admitted on November 8 to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed and alleged Chinese spy, leading to his resignation four days later amid allegations of improper relationships with Nvidia employees. Analysts now point to several reasons investors may reconsider buying the stock, including trust and accountability concerns, board leadership questions, US national security worries tied to external investigations such as a reported probe by the Securities and Exchange Commission, customer financing practices, long-term demand for its chips, and the AI business model itself - all of which predate the scandal. Nvidia's ascent was exceptionally rapid: its share of the S&P 500 rose from 1% in December 2022 to 8.5% by May this year, driven by surging chip demand from hyperscalers and neocloud AI partners that Nvidia has often helped finance. Interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress described a "disciplined" approach on Tuesday's earnings call, saying the company would be selective in capital commitments, investments, and guarantees, though she noted there are no plans to change its backstops for neocloud companies. If that stance shifts, firms like CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital - whose shares have already fallen steeply recently - could decline further. A Bank for International Settlements report published last month examined this vendor-financing trend, finding that between 2021 and 2025 nearly 30% of all AI firms' investment deals by value involved an AI firm on the other side, while 55% of incoming investments in AI firms came from other AI firms. The authors warned these circular relationships can artificially inflate demand, which could become a problem if revenue growth and real end-user demand slow; the AI flywheel could then reverse, potentially causing significant financial market volatility. They also noted many deals are opaque, complex, and private, making them hard to monitor, with risks amplified by growing use of private credit and special purpose vehicles that can create hidden leverage and interconnected exposures during downturns. The article closes by noting the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has dropped nearly 30% over six weeks, suggesting Nvidia's results were not bright enough to mask deep-rooted concerns about the AI ecosystem.
items.title: Nvidia's Strong Q3 Results Amid Deepening Structural Concerns

items.summary: Anthropic, an artificial intelligence firm based in San Francisco that did not exist five years ago, is preparing to ring the opening bell at the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The debut is priced at $83 per share and carries a valuation that eclipses the combined market capitalization of India's ten largest companies. Uday Kotak, Founder and Director of Kotak Mahindra Bank, took to X (formerly Twitter) to highlight what he described as a stark valuation gap between Silicon Valley's AI boom and Indian equities, noting that Anthropic did not exist five years ago.
items.title: Uday Kotak flags valuation gap as Anthropic prepares Nasdaq IPO

items.summary: At Nvidia's first all-hands meeting since founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned, interim CEO Colette Kress addressed employees with the message "let's move forward," according to CNBC reporting that cited attendees present at the roughly one-hour session. The company also announced early pay increases for staff. The meeting was held in person and streamed via Microsoft Teams. It took place a day after Huang offered to return as CEO if the board chose to accept his offer, though he had already stepped down following allegations of at least two affairs. Kress, Nvidia's finance chief, was named interim leader in connection with that departure.
items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO reassures staff amid Jensen Huang departure

items.summary:
A week of widespread technology failures across the United States may trace back to a surge in security patches driven by artificial intelligence, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. The Washington Sun reported that Wall Street executives and NSA representatives told lawmakers these disruptions stemmed from attempts to patch vulnerabilities identified by AI models rather than from cyberattacks; instead, the fixes themselves temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were meant to protect. A congressional official explained that AI is identifying massive vulnerabilities so quickly it increases urgency to patch immediately, with organizations pushing through many patches at once in ways exceeding what their systems can handle.

The underlying logic is that companies and government agencies have turned powerful AI models on their own networks to find weak spots before attackers do, but since adversaries now have access to similar tools or will soon, the pressure has pushed banks, tech firms, and intelligence agencies to deploy fixes faster than usual. The scale of this activity grew sharply: Microsoft fixed about 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update last month, a record, compared with roughly 170 a year earlier; The Wall Street Journal tied the jump partly to AI bug-hunting models including Anthropic's Mythos and similar tools from OpenAI. Serious vulnerabilities have since surfaced in PHP, the Linux operating system, and Java.

The NSA provided the clearest illustration: its classified NSANet network went offline on Tuesday after a software patch for major PHP flaws discovered last month. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the outage was not a cyberattack or coordinated nation-state action but rather many people patching their systems at once, noting that employees were told to stagger arrivals and that the network had been unstable for weeks.

Not every failure fit this pattern. Microsoft's Outlook outage on Thursday affected more than 450 million users over nearly 24 hours and was traced to a latent bug in networking gateway servers dating back to July; The Wall Street Journal reported it separately from the AI patching narrative. The FAA's nationwide ground stop on Friday followed data flooding its network at about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, with a new router at an El Dorado, Arkansas site among suspects; roughly 3,500 planes landed safely while airlines cancelled around 12,462 flights that day. Chase reported on Monday that a software bug slowed transactions and spilled over to other banks and Zelle payments.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has asked the administration to brief Congress, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials are pushing new technology onto old computer systems in ways that overwhelm them, warning that more such incidents will likely occur as new technology rolls out. The Washington Sun cited three sources familiar with private conversations for its reporting.
items.title: US Officials Attribute Tech Outages to AI-Driven Security Patching

items.summary:
Anthropic closed its initial public offering on Wednesday (Nov 18) with a price of US$83 per share, above the range it had targeted and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion. The deal raised US$81.31 billion through an upsized issue of about 980 million shares, roughly 19 per cent more than its original plan to sell 825 million shares between US$70 and US$78 apiece. It also raised US$26 billion in a private placement at the IPO price. On a fully diluted basis the valuation is about US$1.5 trillion, including stock options and restricted stock; on a non-diluted basis it stands at about US$1.1 trillion. The offering made Anthropic the largest stock-market debut on record, surpassing SpaceX's earlier deal, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters in a 22-bank syndicate. Shares are expected to begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker ANT.

The IPO followed a roadshow that drew demand several times the number of shares offered, even amid questions about Anthropic's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as AI competition intensifies. The company is the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to go public, following SpaceX's June offering, while OpenAI is also expected to pursue a listing as early as next year.

Anthropic's growth has been driven by demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code among software developers. Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up about US$10 billion from Sep 30. It reported 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 a year earlier.

Sustaining that growth is proving costly. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, roughly four times the prior-year amount, plus an additional US$5 billion in third-quarter costs, which reduced revenue per dollar of compute. Revenue rose 47 per cent to US$16.96 billion in the third quarter from the second quarter. Operating income turned into a loss of US$567 million after operating profit of US$974 million the prior quarter, while net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion earlier, partly due to convertible bonds.

The company has committed nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google. Its prospectus warned that some providers depend on third-party financing or credit support for chips and capacity, so if such support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity could be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. Investors have grown concerned about debt-fueled AI infrastructure expansion.

Anthropic also faces questions over balancing commercial ambitions with its emphasis on safety; CEO Dario Amodei has urged the industry to slow model development and release, warning advances may outstrip society's ability to manage risks. The company said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research decisions as models take on more work.

Competition is intensifying: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by Ramp in September, versus about 8 per cent for Anthropic's Claude Fable. OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate passed US$40 billion in July, though Anthropic led at the time. A Capgemini study found 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets, and Meta has reportedly reduced its reliance on Anthropic's models while building internal capabilities.

Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion before the IPO, said his bet is that value will accrue to whoever stays at the frontier, arguing Anthropic arguably has the highest probability of remaining there. The prospectus also warned models could develop capabilities faster than the company can evaluate them and put safeguards in place, increasing harm risk; Anthropic noted it may increase human oversight as models take on more work.
items.title: Anthropic completes record $81 billion IPO at ~$1.5 trillion valuation

items.summary: Monetary Authority of Singapore managing director Chia Der Jiun warned consumers to avoid giving artificial intelligence agents their financial account login credentials, citing insufficient safeguards to ensure such tools act safely and within users' instructions. Speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival on Nov 19, he noted that some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, while many have yet to establish terms or channels for agents to access financial services. Chia raised concerns about accountability, asking who bears responsibility if an agent transacts incorrectly or beyond its instructions, since the institution cannot always confirm whether it is acting with full customer authorisation. He said a trusted protocol and secure channel are needed for AI agents to access financial services, drawing on lessons from the first phase of MAS' Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) initiative. Those include giving agents sufficient autonomy while operating within clearly defined boundaries, establishing their identities and authority to act on behalf of users, and specifying instructions along with any limits and conditions. Chia stated that the greater an agent's discretion and impact, the stronger the assurance and controls required. As part of a new phase of SAFR, MAS will develop a common "know your agent" protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions, providing details on who the agent is, whom it represents, its authority, mandate, origins and reliability so that institutions can determine permitted terms and scope and establish a dedicated secure channel. Separately, MAS will set up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to bring together AI agents and programmable money across two use cases: corporate treasury management, where banks could allow an agent to monitor liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds move, and execute permitted actions using tokenised deposits; and payment services, where customer agents could execute instructions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins. In both cases, companies would set the mandates while participating banks would apply controls before executing transactions. Chia said these use cases would provide lessons on the benefits and safeguards of such transactions, adding that consumers and businesses must retain meaningful control over their agents' objectives, mandate and actions, with autonomy bounded and outcomes accountable.
items.title: MAS Chief Warns Against Sharing Financial Login Details With AI Agents

items.summary:
Australian employment fell for a second straight month in October, dropping by 43,500 from September when it had already fallen by a revised 36,400. The combined two-month decline of about 80,000 jobs was the largest such total over five years and far below analysts' forecast of roughly a 25,000 job gain; the October losses were driven mostly by part-time positions. The unemployment rate rose to 4.9%, its highest since October 2021, up from 4.7% the prior month, reaching a level the Reserve Bank of Australia had not expected until late next year when economists had anticipated it holding steady. Krishna Bhimavarapu of State Street Investment Management noted that after higher rates first pressured housing and other rate-sensitive sectors, the slowdown was now appearing clearly in the labour market, strengthening the case that policy is gaining traction and raising the hurdle for another near-term hike.

The soft data bolstered expectations that interest rates have peaked. After five increases in 2026 lifted the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, markets stopped pricing in further rises and began expecting lower rates in the second half of 2027, with about 46 basis points of easing now priced by year-end, double what had been expected before data released on November 19. Citi Australia analysts said that with risks to both unemployment and inflation forecasts skewed softer, they expect the RBA to hold at 4.85% until Q3 2027 when it could begin moving back toward neutral, while acknowledging a residual risk of another hike.

The reaction hit currency and bond markets: the Australian dollar fell about 0.5% as it reached an 11-month low of 66.80 US cents, though this was described in the source as its tenth-lowest level over ten months; three-year government bond futures rallied 15 ticks to 95.41, their highest since late August.

Broader labour-market weakness accompanied the headline figures: the participation rate dipped from 66.8% to 66.6%, hours worked fell by 0.2%, and youth unemployment for those aged 15 to 24 rose to 11.3% from 11.1%, its highest in five years. Anecdotal evidence of wider layoffs is building, including a union report that David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs after entering administration on November 18, joining other job losses at Australian firms as the economy slows.

The source carries an AI-generated label and includes anecdotal elements such as the David Jones collapse and RBA board members' private risk warnings. The dollar's level is reported with some ambiguity regarding whether it was its tenth-lowest over ten months or fell to a new low of 66.80 US cents.
items.title: Australia's jobless rate hits five-year high as markets price 2027 rate cuts

items.summary: At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Elon Musk elaborated on his disapproval of Nvidia's board decision to remove founder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about a series of extramarital affairs. Comparing Huang to Michael Jordan, Musk said ousting him is like 'kicking Michael Jordan off your team' when the company was winning, arguing it would not be good for shareholders. He called Huang one of history's most talented entrepreneur-CEOs and stated he would hire him himself if asked about his X post. Musk also signed a petition with over 200,000 other people urging Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO, though the board confirmed it has no plans to bring Huang back. He emphasized that there is no one who can replace Huang, citing decades of relationships and personal loyalty from employees who have declined higher offers elsewhere. Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey echoed this view, saying 'China wants Jensen out,' while noting the decision knocked a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market cap. Musk did not express concern over what Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy could mean for U.S. national security, stating he does not think Huang is disloyal to the United States. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its 33-year founder-CEO, with Nadella expressing confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.
items.title: Musk Defends Jensen Huang's Ousting at DealBook Summit

items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella commented on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation, which followed a series of controversies. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Nadella described the situation as tragic and said he wanted to give Huang space to figure things out after their long relationship. Huang stepped down last week from a role he had held for 33 years that was central to Nvidia's rise to one of the world's most valuable companies. His leadership came under scrutiny after reports emerged that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing, as well as affairs with two Nvidia employees, including a direct report. Despite these developments, Nadella said he still has confidence in Nvidia and its close partnership with Microsoft. He pointed to Colette Kress, the interim CEO who worked at Microsoft for a long time, noting that he remains connected to the same people he dealt with before Huang's departure and trusts the team to continue doing good work. Nadella also reflected on how founders like Bill Gates built larger-than-life personas as CEOs but are not gods, observing that companies must eventually have someone take over when they need to succeed.
items.title: Nadella expresses confidence in Nvidia amid Huang's departure

items.summary: Nvidia's shares dipped Wednesday even as the company reported strong earnings, because investors remained uneasy about the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. The stock decline reflected lingering concerns that leadership instability could trigger a talent exodus and undermine confidence in the chipmaker's direction. To address skepticism among employees and investors alike, Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress initiated what has been described as a charm offensive during the company's first employee town hall since Huang's ouster. In addition to expanding stock buybacks, Kress reportedly promised pay raises at that meeting, while also assuring staff that the firm's "passion to innovate" would remain unchanged. The leadership transition has exposed a notable divide between Silicon Valley and Washington: according to a former politico-turned-tech executive speaking with Semafor's Liz Hoffman, observers outside of politics focus on whether Huang will return to Nvidia by Christmas, whereas in Washington the concern centers instead on whether he faces imprisonment.
items.title: Nvidia Shares Fall Despite Strong Earnings Amid Jensen Huang Departure Uncertainty

items.summary: On Wednesday, Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the price range it had initially set for the debut. The higher-than-expected valuation signals strong investor enthusiasm for what is being described as the first frontier AI lab to go public, even amid recent turmoil in tech stocks following a Democratic sweep in midterms and Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia CEO. Analysts note that investors appear to treat Anthropic as a pure-play AI company, distinguishing it at a time when sentiment toward AI infrastructure and hardware is cooling. The debut could attract roughly $250 million in net retail buying, potentially double SpaceX's record of $118 million in retail purchases.
items.title: Anthropic prices IPO above target range

items.summary: Nvidia executive Jay Puri has become personally entangled in an unfolding scandal involving his wife, Cenly Chen, a former senior executive of Super Micro Computer (Supermicro). US prosecutors have charged Supermicro executives with conspiring to smuggle $2.5 billion worth of servers containing Nvidia chips to Chinese customers. The Information reported Wednesday that Puri and Chen had told colleagues about their marriage this year, noting that Chen was part of the team managing Supermicro's relationship with Nvidia, though the company has disputed her alleged role in chip allocations. This development follows a report Tuesday by Muddy Waters Research, an influential short-selling firm founded in 2010 by American investor Carson Block, which disclosed it was shorting Nvidia shares and raised questions about Puri-Chen ties. The firm's report, titled NVIDIA: More China, cited photographs from 2024 to 2026 showing Puri alongside a woman identified variously as Cenly Chen and Cenly Puri. It referenced an October shareholder lawsuit alleging that Chen had managed Supermicro's acquisition of GPU chips from Nvidia and decided how to distribute NVDA GPUs among the company's customers, asserting there was no way she lacked knowledge of its illicit sales. At Nvidia, Puri became executive vice-president of Worldwide Field Operations in 2009, overseeing global sales, business development, partnerships and customer relationships; he announced his retirement from that operational role in June but continues as a senior adviser, though reports indicate an uneasy relationship with the company. According to media reports citing insiders, Jensen Huang reportedly berated Puri during a closed-door meeting attended by more than 30 executives in February, telling him he hoped Puri would get the flu and die before adding that his death would put them all out of their misery; Puri reportedly remained silent. Muddy Waters made its reputation investigating Chinese companies listed in Western markets, notably exposing alleged accounting fraud at Sino-Forest, and publishes investigative reports while taking positions in scrutinized shares, giving it a financial interest in Nvidia's share price declining here. The controversy unfolds against an increasingly charged American political climate marked by suspicion of foreign connections, particularly Chinese ones, even as Silicon Valley remains built on international talent, with Indian-origin executives including Satya Nadella of Microsoft, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet and Arvind Krishna of IBM leading some of America's most powerful corporations. Nvidia's crisis has also escalated sharply, with chairman Harvey Jones delivering a decisive rebuff to growing pressure to bring back Huang as CEO, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate him; Huang is expected to face congressional questioning on December 1.
items.title: Jay Puri's Ties to Supermicro Exec Amid Nvidia Scandal

items.summary: Following a Monday (Nov 16) announcement that the United States would tighten exports of advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil on suspicion these countries could serve as routes for diverting chips to China, Indonesia is reviewing the measure's impact. The new rules require companies to obtain US government licences to export, re-export or transfer certain advanced AI chips to the five affected countries, and also apply to overseas data centres that supply large computing capacity to firms headquartered in China, Russia, Iran, Cuba and other nations subject to US controls. Indonesia's Government Communications Agency (GCA) said on Wednesday (Nov 18) it is seeking industry input on how the restrictions affect operations and investment, including in the data centre sector, while remaining open to technical dialogue with counterparts to clarify application and support continued access to advanced computing for legitimate commercial use. M Habib Abiyan Dzakwan of CSIS Indonesia warned that investors from Western countries would grow more cautious, noting that firms previously had only needed to comply with Indonesian regulations but now must also satisfy US requirements; he added the restrictions might not drive investment away entirely but could complicate AI and data centre investments through additional regulatory burdens. Dyah Ayu of CELIOS cautioned that investors may wait for greater clarity on licensing rules, postpone final decisions or build capacity gradually before committing further to AI hardware spending. Citing figures from the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, the GCA reported Indonesia's semiconductor device and electronic integrated circuit exports reached approximately US$ 4.1 billion in 2025, up from US$1.5 billion in 2024. Habib suggested the government examine AI chip import data to gauge volumes, sectors involved and operating data centres, which could help address US diversion concerns, while also coordinating with Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand on their responses and strengthening enforcement against illegal diversion. Maria Monica Wihardja of ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute noted that Indonesia is the only affected Southeast Asian country without a dedicated strategic trade management framework, relying instead on a patchwork of customs, import-export and sector-specific regulations; she warned this absence weakens export controls by allowing imported goods to be loosely re-exported elsewhere with unclear legal consequences. Dyah emphasized a deeper risk: domestic operators may struggle to build their own capacity and become mere customers of global providers, increasing Indonesia's dependence on foreign technology as a consumer. The GCA said it is developing a framework to facilitate legitimate trade while reducing the risk of dual-use goods being diverted or misused, reflecting its commitment to an open, predictable and trusted environment and supporting President Prabowo Subianto's direction to develop the semiconductor industry and strengthen Indonesia's role in global supply chains.
items.title: Indonesia reviews US AI chip export curbs amid analyst warnings

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping stated on Thursday that China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation. He made the remarks at the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. Xi added that China is ready to work with all parties to build the pillars supporting an Asia-Pacific community.
items.title: Xi positions China as leader of APEC cooperation

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for continued efforts to build an Asia-Pacific community characterized by solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, and innovation and inclusive development. He made the remarks at the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province. Xi urged strengthening shared interests, working together to address difficulties and challenges, and fostering a sense of community among regional parties. He emphasized the importance of innovation in building this community, calling for encouragement of science and technology exchanges and cooperation, facilitation of the use of innovation outcomes, and cultivation of an open, fair, just, and non-discriminatory environment for cooperation. Xi also stressed upholding openness and integration by advancing economic integration steadily across the Asia-Pacific region. He called on all parties to promote free and open trade and investment, remove bottlenecks in factor flows, and ensure smooth economic circulation throughout the region.
items.title: Xi Jinping Calls for Further Efforts to Build an Asia-Pacific Community

items.summary: Worldwide equities declined on Wednesday, November 18, after Nvidia's quarterly report and ahead of Anthropic's planned market debut. The fall was compounded by a stronger US dollar driven by comments from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, who told CNBC that the central bank must either approve a half-point rate hike at its December meeting or signal a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Mining stocks weighed on European shares, while Nvidia's results initially lifted Asian markets with South Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight; however, the rally faded and Nvidia fell 2.9 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board rejected rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week, leaving uncertainty unresolved. Neil Shah of Counterpoint noted that Tuesday's results had stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff but postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety. In US markets, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 per cent to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 0.23 per cent to 7,323.63, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42 per cent to 24,429.89. The MSCI global gauge fell 0.45 per cent to 1,074.61, while Europe's STOXX 600 dropped 1.03 per cent and emerging market stocks slipped 0.2 per cent; Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent to 59,024.28. The dollar index climbed 0.17 per cent to a fresh 19-month high of 103.79, with the euro down 0.22 per cent at $1.0973. Juan Perez of Monex USA said traders believe the Federal Reserve is determined to hike rates and possibly do so aggressively, which was carrying the dollar higher. Crude prices fell after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, adding supply-surplus expectations: US crude lost 3.3 per cent to $83.17 a barrel while Brent dropped 1.4 per cent to $91.84 a barrel. Spot gold declined 3.24 per cent to $3,725.10 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.98 per cent to $45.04 an ounce; copper slipped 4.54 per cent to $12,626.00 a ton. Yields on 2-year US Treasury notes edged higher by 1.31 basis points to 4.802 per cent as hawkish Fed comments and minutes from the last policy meeting underscored inflation concerns, while the benchmark 10-year note yield fell 3.47 basis points to 5.068 per cent.
items.title: Global stocks slip on Nvidia results and hawkish Fed as dollar hits fresh high

items.summary:
Bharatiya Janata Party leader Tejasvi Surya stated that Grand Theft Auto VI has a significant India connection, with much of its development carried out by Rockstar India's studio in Bengaluru. In an X post, he noted that more than 1,600 developers at the Bengaluru studio had worked on the game and described it as one of the most awaited games worldwide. Surya also traced the studio's origins to Dhruva Interactive, which was founded by Rajesh Rao in Bengaluru in 1995 with a single computer. He called this company India's first game development studio and said it was acquired by Rockstar Games in 2019. Surya observed that while Bengaluru is widely recognised for its IT industry, the city's gaming ecosystem represents another facet of its technology sector.

The article provides background on why GTA remains a major franchise, reporting through AP that publisher Take-Two Interactive says the Grand Theft Auto series has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. The series began in 1997 with a top-down game and evolved into an open-world crime franchise despite repeated controversies. Its previous main instalment, Grand Theft Auto V, released in 2013 and accounts for more than 230 million of those sales; the article also states that this game generated $1 billion in retail sales within its first three days of release.

Regarding what to expect from GTA 6, the piece reports it follows a 13-year gap since the previous main instalment. The game is set to return players to Vice City, the franchise's fictional setting inspired by Miami, and features two protagonists while continuing the open-world crime narrative. It has received eight nominations at the 2026 Game Awards, including Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Audio Design, Best Action/Adventure and Best Performance. The awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on December 10.
items.title: BJP leader Tejasvi Surya credits Bengaluru studio for GTA 6 development

items.summary: According to National Health Accounts (NHA) Estimates for 2023-24, government health expenditure per person varies sharply across Indian regions. The four poorer northern states of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand averaged around Rs 1,651 in per capita spending, which is less than half the Rs 3,501 recorded for the northeastern states and nearly a fourth of the Rs 7,209 average for union territories. Senior Assistant Editor Anuja Jaiswal at The Times of India noted that fixed costs such as capital investment and infrastructure remain relatively high even when the number of people using those services is limited.
items.title: Regional healthcare spending gaps in India
