items.summary: In a double murder trial before Justice Natalie Adams, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC told the court that Beau Lamarre-Condon's "wounded pride" after his breakup with Jesse Baird led him to plan revenge. The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner Luke Davies at Baird's Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024, using a police Glock while disguised as an Uber Eats driver. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter, with the trial entering its ninth week. Hatfield argued that Lamarre-Condon was infatuated, obsessed and insecure about his relationship with Baird from late 2022 when they began casually dating, pointing to testimony from friends who said he watched Baird have sex with other men, broke into his home for his phone and followed him in a car. Hatfield called this "classic stalking" and described the subsequent break-in as astonishing conduct for a serving officer driven by sexual jealousy. The prosecution argued that after Baird ended things for good in November 2023, Lamarre-Condon wanted to harm him and devised the plan to enter his home disguised as an Uber Eats driver. The defence contends both men died in struggles while Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence, claiming he aimed only at Baird's shoulder to make him drop a knife before accidentally firing twice as they fell. Hatfield countered that forensic evidence shows the first shot struck Baird in the back as he fled toward the rear door and that the near-vertical bullet trajectory through the floor indicates a controlled, execution-style shot to the temple. He argued the timing between shots allowed only two to three steps rather than the wrestling described by Lamarre-Condon, and that Davies was killed by a bullet passing through the door into his head, evidenced by gunshot stippling on the door but not the body. Hatfield noted that key elements of the defence case came solely from Lamarre-Condon's own testimony, with nothing independent to support them.The trial continues.
items.title: Crown alleges wounded pride drove Lamarre-Condon to murder Baird and Davies

items.summary: Bernard Kearney, director of BK Labour Hire, continued his evidence on Thursday before the royal commission investigating alleged corruption in Victoria's construction sector. The company held an enterprise bargaining agreement with the CFMEU that helped it secure lucrative contracts on Big Build projects from around 2022. In September 2025, industry regulator the Labour Hire Authority scrutinized BK Labour over cash withdrawals totalling $77,970 and transfers to entities in the name of former senior CFMEU organiser Joe Myles, totalling $127,472. Rather than provide a statutory declaration explaining those transactions as requested, Kearney admitted he had asked for fake invoices to be created. The fabricated invoices covered sponsorships worth thousands of dollars to the Kangaroos Junior football club, Parkdale Vultures football and netball club, Yarra Jets Junior football club, and Port Melbourne bowling club. Kearney maintained that Myles was paid through his companies for work performed, describing him as an asset for knowledge on health and safety procedures. When asked why he had not simply told the Labour Hire Authority this himself, Kearney replied that he could not answer. The commission heard Wednesday that BK Labour received a succession of invoices from Myles totalling $256,000 over about a year; Myles was sacked by the union in mid-2024. When shown one fake invoice bearing handwriting, Kearney initially claimed it was his own but admitted under questioning that it was not when asked to demonstrate his handwriting on plain paper. Commissioner Chris Kourakis accused him of deliberately withholding information and suggested he was trying to protect business partner Duane Allen; Kearney denied this. On Wednesday, Kearney was also questioned about $165,000 paid to union-aligned Bandidos gang member Joel Leavitt, whom the company said had provided no work for the firm. Kearney admitted paying it and moving on but could not explain why, while counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr suggested only a couple of possible reasons remained: fear of violence or suppression of information Leavitt held about them; Kearney answered that neither applied. No visual was warranted as the figures are separate transactions rather than comparable values across names.
items.title: BK Labour Hire boss admits to fake sponsorship invoices at Big Build royal commission

items.summary: Cruise operator StarDream Cruises announced on Thursday (Nov 19) that its Star Voyager ship will operate under a three-year seasonal deployment based in Singapore, running through 2029. The arrangement was made in partnership with the Singapore Tourism Board (STB), and is expected to provide travellers with more cruise itineraries across Southeast Asia while attracting regional and international fly-cruise visitors who sail from Singapore. Expanded sailings will carry guests to destinations including Jakarta, Krabi, Phuket, Melaka, Langkawi, Penang, Port Klang in Kuala Lumpur, and Pulau Pangkor. The Star Voyager has a passenger capacity of about 2,000 across more than 970 staterooms, with onboard amenities that include a water park, numerous bars and restaurants, a casino, and a theatre. Michael Goh, president of StarDream Cruises, said in a statement that Singapore has been an important market for the cruise line's operations for more than 30 years, noting that this seasonal deployment builds on its long-standing presence there while contributing to Singapore's growth as a leading regional cruise hub. Jean Ng, assistant chief executive of STB's experience development group, added that the three-year deployment runs alongside Genting Dream's year-round sailings and reflects continued confidence in Singapore as a cruise gateway for travellers discovering Asia.
items.title: StarDream Cruises deploys Star Voyager in three-year seasonal program at Singapore

items.summary: Seven Russian figure skaters have been barred from this week's Finlandia Trophy in Helsinki after Finnish authorities moved to prevent athletes holding Russian passports from entering the country. The Russian Figure Skating Federation announced on Tuesday that these seven competitors, including Olympic pairs medalists Anastasia Mishina and Aleksandr Galliamov, would be unable to travel to Finland as a result of the entry restriction. This development threatens their chances of qualifying for the Grand Prix Final. According to Finnish government statements issued by Monday, Russian citizens holding Schengen visas are now permitted into Finland only for work deemed essential to national interests, with sports explicitly excluded from that allowance.
items.title: Russian Skaters Denied Entry to Finlandia Trophy

items.summary: At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Chinese leader Xi Jinping greeted Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi with a handshake on Thursday for the second consecutive day. This marked their first face-to-face contact more than a year into a standoff between the two countries. The leaders' initial encounter had taken place at a welcome banquet a day earlier, and they appeared to speak for some length afterward, though the substance of her remarks was not immediately clear. For Japanese officials, even customary diplomatic courtesy such as a handshake had become a matter of suspense, with attention focused on whether Beijing would extend routine protocol to Takaichi. The meeting followed comments made by Takaichi last November regarding possible Japanese military intervention in a Taiwan crisis.
items.title: Takaichi and Xi exchange handshakes at APEC summit amid protocol tensions

items.summary:
A Russian official reports that Ukraine has attacked the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a single week. Sergei Aksyonov, Moscow's appointed head of Crimea, confirmed via Telegram on Thursday morning that traffic was temporarily suspended after another strike and said damage assessment was underway. The bridge had already been hit twice earlier this week, with one attack causing severe damage and part of it collapsing into the water. Ukraine has long targeted the infrastructure because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

The latest news arrives as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for talks in China. Separately, Ukrainian sources issued air raid alerts overnight for districts just outside Kyiv, while at least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday; the regional state administration described that strike as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November, bringing down a key section of the road. That portion of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed after being brought down by Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before." While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge permanently, recent attempts are described as bringing them closer to destroying its crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading toward the front line. Russian forces have also targeted key crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv recently; strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges, causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system, and some power and water outages.
items.title: Crimean Bridge struck for third time this week, Russian official says

items.summary: NSW One Nation Legislative Council candidate Katherine Deves argued that high rates of welfare use among certain migrant groups justify deep cuts to migration, citing a graph she posted showing working-age welfare recipients by country of birth. In an interview with Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings, Ms Deves claimed up to 24 per cent of some overseas-born cohorts were on welfare and cited concerns about pressure on the NDIS, health, education, and housing systems. The graph she used shows Sudan, Iraq, and Syria as having the highest rates in Australia and cites Department of Social Services and Bureau of Statistics longitudinal data sets as its source, but does not explain the methodology behind the figures. Peter Whiteford, director of the Social Policy Institute at the Australian National University, told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings that the chart was "very misleading" and described it as "completely wrong," adding that most of the numbers were "puzzling to say the least." During the interview Ms Deves also endorsed fellow NSW One Nation candidate Stuart Bonds over comments at an anti-immigration rally suggesting white Australians are being demographically replaced, which she dismissed as a conspiracy theory. New South Wales Premier Chris Minns called her remarks horrifying and said they demonised Middle Eastern Australians and others who have contributed to the state by starting families, building businesses, and joining communities. Ms Deves was contacted for comment.
items.title: ANU researcher rejects One Nation candidate's migrant welfare graph

items.summary: The Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd (MCL) public issue opened on November 19, 2026, and remains open until November 23, 2026. The book-built offer comprises 66.18 crore equity shares and is entirely an offer for sale by existing shareholders, meaning the company will receive no proceeds while all funds go to selling shareholders. The basis of allotment was expected to be finalised on November 25, 2026, with tentative listing on BSE and NSE scheduled for November 27. MCL set a price band of Rs 129-136 per share (face value Rs 2), corresponding to 64.50 times the face value at the floor and 68 times at the upper end. The lot size is 110 shares, with retail investors needing Rs 14,960 to bid one lot at the top of the band. Grey market sentiment was modest: a premium of around Rs 3 per share (nearly 2% over the Rs 136 upper price band) implied an estimated listing price near Rs 139 and a potential gain of about 2.2%, though such premiums are unofficial indicators that do not guarantee returns. Brokerage firm Anand Rathi rated the issue 'Subscribe - Long Term', citing MCL's status as India's largest single coal producer, strong profitability, substantial reserves, mechanised opencast operations, integrated rail and port evacuation infrastructure, long-term Fuel Supply Agreements, and backing from parent Coal India Ltd. The company reported its highest profit after tax among Coal India's listed subsidiaries in FY26, with an operating EBITDA margin of 41.7% and return on net worth of 53.8%. At the upper price band, MCL was valued at 8.4 times its FY26 P/E and 5.9 times FY26 EV/EBITDA, implying a post-issue market capitalisation of Rs 9,00,097 million. On financials, total income rose 3% year-on-year to Rs 33,899 crore in FY26 from Rs 33,029 crore in FY25, while profit after tax declined 1% to Rs 10,698 crore from Rs 10,825 crore. Incorporated in April 1992 as a wholly owned subsidiary of Coal India Ltd, MCL operates primarily in non-coking coal across Odisha's Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields, with customers spanning power generation plus cement, steel, aluminium, sponge iron and paper sectors. As of June 30, 2026, it operated 17 mines (14 opencast and three underground) and runs the 10-million-tonne-per-annum Ib Valley Coal Washery; as of September 30, 2026, it employed 20,526 permanent staff. Anand Rathi flagged risks including concentration in non-coking coal, heavy dependence on thermal power sector and government-owned utilities, customer and contractor concentration, regulatory and environmental challenges, and the gradual shift toward renewable energy. The article's brokerage views are attributed to an SEBI-registered research analyst and are not those of The Economic Times Digital.
items.title: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO opens for subscription

items.summary: Fiona, a hippo at Cincinnati Zoo born prematurely in 2017 and named after the Shrek character, has been under round-the-clock medical care for about nine days after swallowing a knitted hat. According to zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley, a child tossed the cap into the air near her enclosure when a ceiling fan caught it and propelled it through a small opening above the viewing window. Initially appearing unharmed, staff noticed Fiona's appetite declining and placed her under constant supervision. She underwent a colonoscopy earlier in the week, but officials are hoping to help her pass the object naturally rather than surgically. Surgery has been ruled out on expert advice that it is not an option for fully grown hippos. To encourage movement through her digestive tract, zoo staff borrowed a vibration plate from a nearby horse farm and have had Fiona stand on it several times daily. They are also keeping her hydrated, administering pain medication, feeding her favourite foods, and offering her the scent of coffee, which she has always liked. Dr Wenninger noted that an ultrasound performed Wednesday gave staff optimism that the hat was beginning to pass through her small intestine, adding that Fiona is large enough for a smallish hat to move through. He said the team can only provide supportive care at this point and may need another procedure in the future. When she was born weighing 13 kilograms, Fiona became the smallest hippo known to survive premature birth, with typical birth weights ranging between 25 and 54kg for the species. The article also references a Washington man who was disembowelled by a hippo protecting her young on an African safari last year, as well as the earlier incident involving gorilla Harambe being shot after a three-year-old boy climbed into his enclosure eight months prior.
items.title: Cincinnati Zoo Hippo Fiona Undergoes Treatment After Swallowing a Hat

items.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Vanuatu's Environment Minister Ralph Regenvanu called for reform of the UN climate summit process as talks entered their final days. He accused a small group of states of blocking progress at both climate summits and other multilateral negotiations, including the plastics treaty that began under the UN in 2022 but has yet to make progress. The COP operates by consensus, though some countries such as Panama are pushing for majority voting to break deadlocks. Regenvanu named specific blockers: "the Arab bloc and the LMDCs," which he described as a group of around twenty developing countries including Saudi Arabia and India, plus Russia. He also cited US President Donald Trump's withdrawal from climate negotiations, noting that the United States is again absent this year, while acknowledging multiple geopolitical tensions affecting discussions in Antalya. Regenvanu leads Vanuatu's negotiations on climate issues, over a plastics treaty, and at the International Court of Justice, where Vanuatu secured an advisory opinion on climate last year. He acknowledged a deep gap between developed and developing countries on finance but said vulnerable nations must try to build bridges. As part of the Alliance of Small Island States, whose members face rising sea levels and intensifying storms, Regenvanu warned there is a real risk that COP31 could reverse previously agreed commitments as issues thought settled return to the table.
items.title: Vanuatu Minister Calls for UN Climate Summit Reform Amid Backsliding Fears

items.summary: A former McDonald's worker named Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023 and is now 22, has called on the firm to change how it treats younger employees. She says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers during a night shift, telling her to "just suck it up and deal with it." Hope also reported seeing older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers and discussing wanting to sleep with them once they turned 18. She described the branch as having a very sexualised, toxic environment, recounting an incident in which a manager put his hands on her shoulders from behind, after which she said she "moved quick" whenever he approached. Her main concern was for younger teenagers, whom she says were not being looked after and who appeared to be waiting for their 18th birthdays under what she described as a toxic culture where the feeling prevailed that it was no longer illegal because they had aged out of child status. Hope said "That is literally a child still." She joined hundreds of current and former workers bringing discrimination claims against McDonald's, which are being presented by law firm Leigh Day. This week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can proceed to a full hearing expected in April; the BBC understands these relate to indirect discrimination rather than sexual harassment. Hope said she was not taking part for money and hoped the case would change how McDonald's treats allegations, shake up its internal process, make life easier for young people starting their first jobs, and improve safety. She accused the company of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have claims struck out, which Judge Glennie rejected. A McDonald's spokesperson declined to comment on ongoing legal proceedings but said the company had embedded robust safeguarding initiatives as part of its commitment to staff, that any harassment or discrimination is unacceptable, and that it has industry-leading measures in place with external experts.
items.title: McDonald's workers bring discrimination claims over sexualised workplace

items.summary: Contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index rose 0.9% while those for the S&P 500 climbed 0.5%. This followed Anthropic pricing its initial public offering at $83 per share, making it the biggest first-time share sale on record. Asian equities were mixed early in trading: Japan's Nikkei 225 index was little changed, while Australian shares fell more than 1% as commodity prices declined. Copper plunged Wednesday amid a broad selloff as bullish investors exited positions tied to the AI boom; copper dropped 5.7% on the LME to its lowest level since April, and tin shed 5% in London. Gold tumbled over 3% in the prior session to its lowest point in more than a year after Federal Reserve officials argued for additional interest-rate hikes. Anthropic's listing arrives at a pivotal moment for markets, with Nvidia tumbling recently following Jensen Huang's ouster and growing concerns that technology spending may slow; the IPO serves as a test of whether investors will commit fresh capital to the sector amid deteriorating sentiment. Kyle Rodda of Capital.com described it as "a barometer for how bullish the market really is on AI names," while Dilin Wu of Pepperstone noted that successful pricing does not guarantee shares will rise once trading begins. Investors also reviewed minutes from the Fed's October meeting, which indicated nearly all officials agreed they would likely need to raise rates in coming months to return inflation to their 2% target, with two policymakers suggesting an increase exceeding 25 basis points could be warranted in December if incoming data proved unfavorable. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly called for a measured approach and said "we'll have to further tighten interest rates," while Governor Michael Barr stated higher borrowing costs would likely be appropriate.
items.title: Anthropic IPO and Fed tightening expectations weigh on markets amid mixed Asian equities

items.summary: Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is facing mounting scrutiny over his leadership after Cameron Bancroft, banned for nine months in the 2018 'Sandpapergate' ball-tampering scandal, broke his silence with a detailed public account. In an explosive column of about 4,497 words published Wednesday, Bancroft called Cummins' repeated denials of knowledge over eight years the "final straw" that prompted him to speak out, while describing himself as relieved and liberated after carrying the burden for so long. He reiterated claims that the wider Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plan during the 2018 South Africa tour, acknowledging David Warner had raised the idea of using sandpaper on Day 2's tea break in Port Elizabeth, with bowling coach David Saker and then head coach Darren Lehmann present. Cummins has maintained his position unchanged since day one, a stance reinforced by manager Neil Maxwell, who urged people to read Pat's interview transcript and noted Bancroft had been through a lot. The controversy intensified calls for an immediate review of Cummins' captaincy from prominent writer Robert Craddock in The Australian, while broader media questioned whether he could continue as Test skipper amid renewed scrutiny. Bancroft's account reopened wounds from the Cape Town Test, where his sandpaper use led to lengthy bans for him, Warner and then-captain Steve Smith, who was also stripped of the captaincy; the scandal resurfaced after Usman Khawaja's autobiography allegations that the wider team knew about the plan. Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg announced an independent forum allowing players to share their accounts but clarified the body is not seeking a perfect truth or reopening the investigation or imposing fresh sanctions, while former opener Warner said he had nothing further to add and pacer Chadd Sayers questioned whether the process would make complete accounts public. With Bancroft now willing to participate in CA's independent process, Sandpapergate has become once again a major issue for Australian cricket, with Cummins' unchanged denial casting an increasingly uncomfortable test on his leadership.
items.title: Bancroft's revelations intensify pressure on Cummins' captaincy

items.summary: The Hindustan Times published a five-minute morning news brief on November 19 covering politics, national and global events, entertainment, and sports. The lead story reported that US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin were set to hold a trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders' summit in Shenzhen. China stated the three leaders would engage in "in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations." A second story detailed the funeral of slain Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat, held around 10pm Wednesday nearly 160km from his family's one-storey house. In keeping with government policy against handing over bodies of slain terrorists to families and preventing public funerals that could glorify militants, Bhat's body was buried in a village in the Bangus valley of Jammu and Kashmir's Kupwara district; his family resides in Khrewan village in Kupwara. The entertainment section reported that Grand Theft Auto VI began rolling out Wednesday evening as the global release concluded an eight-year development saga, with Indian users gaining access at midnight Thursday. According to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, GTA VI had booked about $1.5 billion—roughly ₹14,100 crore—in pre-orders by Wednesday, surpassing Avengers: Endgame's 2019 record of $1.2 billion in its first weekend global opening. The sports section covered Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan, which the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said moved northwards at a speed of 5 kmph over the west-central and adjoining central parts of the south Bay of Bengal during the six hours ending 11.30pm on November 18, with landfall expected near Odisha and Andhra Pradesh on November 20. The brief also reported an India vs New Zealand Test match in Wellington where Jasprit Bumrah took two wickets while Anshul Kamboj and Akash Deep each took one; the hosts were reduced to 60/4 at lunch on Day 1, but Henry Nicholls and Rachin Ravindra steadied the innings with a 39-run stand. The document concluded with an editorial statement from the HT News Desk describing its round-the-clock coverage across politics, economy, business, science and technology, environment, law and order, infrastructure, education, climate issues, and geopolitics.
items.title: Hindustan Times morning news brief for November 19

items.summary:
Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata and members of the Tata Group's board are scheduled to visit Air India's headquarters in Gurugram on Thursday, according to people familiar with the matter. The visit is expected to cover both the airline headquarters and its academy, with board members anticipated to review the carrier's performance as it continues posting losses years after the Tata Group acquired it in January 2022. Senior executives attending may include Tata Sons chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran.

Noel Tata was unanimously appointed chairman of Tata Trusts in October 2024, two days after his half-brother Ratan Tata died. The role placed him at the head of the philanthropic institutions that collectively own about 66% of Tata Sons. He has reportedly differed with the Tata Sons board over Chandrasekaran's reappointment for another five-year term, a planned public offering of Tata Sons, and growing losses in new-age businesses including aviation, electric vehicle batteries, digital commerce, and semiconductors.

The visit coincides with Air India's announcement last month that it would establish a full-time team to systematically review expenditure and identify cost-saving opportunities. In his first internal communication to employees seen by Hindustan Times, CEO Tewolde Gebremariam stated in October that cost savings could not be driven by a single team or function but required the active participation of every employee. He emphasized embedding 'a mindset of frugality, accountability, and thoughtful decision-making' alongside operational excellence.

The focus on costs comes amid challenging conditions for airlines, including elevated oil prices amid the West Asia crisis and pressure on fuel bills, margins, and flight routes. Gebremariam announced that a cross-functional Cost Savings Team had been established to systematically review all expenditure across functions, asking employees to extend their 'full support and cooperation' as it works to deliver cost efficiencies organization-wide.
items.title: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata to visit Air India headquarters

items.summary: Odisha has intensified preparations for Severe Cyclone Akvan, which the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast to make landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha by noon on Friday, November 20. Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi said around 50,000 people had already been evacuated from vulnerable areas as of Wednesday evening, with the largest operation underway in Ganjam district; the state has set a target of zero casualties. According to an IMD update at 11:30 pm on November 18, Akvan was centred over the west-central Bay of Bengal about 480 km southeast of Narsapur, 600 km south of Gopalpur and 660 km south of Puri. The storm is expected to move north-northwestwards before crossing the North Andhra Pradesh-Yanam and South Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri, packing sustained winds of 90-100 kmph with gusts reaching 110 kmph. Residents from villages in Ganjam, Gajapati, Kandhamal, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri districts are being shifted to cyclone shelters and relief centres; the state has readied 3,000 cyclone shelters of which 448 were already operational, while Rs 20 crore was allotted to 15 districts for relief and rescue operations. The IMD warned of very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across large parts of southern and coastal Odisha, including Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, Kalahandi, Gajapati, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Boudh, Puri, Nayagarh and Khurda districts, with coastal wind speeds expected to reach around 100 kmph. The government ordered the closure of schools in six districts-Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal-from November 19 to 21 as a precautionary measure, while Khurda district's schools would remain shut for two days; leave was suspended for employees, senior bureaucrats were deployed to vulnerable districts, and recruitment examinations scheduled later that week were postponed. Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said the state's strategy had to be revised after the cyclone changed course, expanding the threat from southern Odisha to coastal districts as well. Authorities identified 141 landslide-prone locations across the state, particularly in Koraput and Malkangiri, and began relocating residents; Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh P Patil directed tourism authorities to implement safety measures for visitors amid forecasts of rough seas, strong winds and coastal inundation. The Puri Jagannath temple administration announced closure of Shree Gundicha Temple until November 21, while fishermen were advised not to venture into the sea. BJD president and former chief minister Naveen Patnaik urged people to remain alert and cooperate with the administration; he recalled Cyclone Arnab's devastation last month, noting that Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal districts were still recovering from damage caused by Arnab. Patnaik criticised the BJP government over its handling of the Ganjam floods, describing them as man-made and demanding accountability, while BJD legislators disrupted Assembly proceedings seeking a discussion on flood management and disaster response; Cyclone Arnab's aftermath had left at least 11 people dead and six others missing in Odisha. The IMD forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall across parts of southern West Bengal between November 19 and 21, affecting Purba Medinipur, Paschim Medinipur, South 24-Parganas, Howrah, Jhargram and Bankura districts; Kolkata was expected to experience thunderstorms and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph. Officials said the cyclone could affect a broad stretch of coastline because of signs of possible recurvature in its track.
items.title: Odisha intensifies evacuations as Cyclone Akvan alters course toward landfall

items.summary: CGTN's First Voice editorial argues that Chinese President Xi Jinping's keynote at the opening of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen was fundamentally a defense of economic openness against an era defined by tariffs, industrial policy and geopolitical rivalry. The column characterizes his message as reassurance to Asia-Pacific economies: support free and open trade and investment, maintain smooth global supply chains, and advance the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. It contends that this language addresses companies facing trade fragmentation as a business risk, which experience geopolitics through higher compliance costs, delayed shipments, duplicated suppliers, uncertain market access and postponed investment decisions rather than abstract theory. The editorial notes Xi's pledge to provide its super-large open market and broad development prospects, describing China as one of the world's largest consumer markets and an indispensable node in many supply chains. It cites figures from the just-concluded China International Import Expo (CIIE), which attracted a record 4,142 exhibitors with intended deals reaching $85.45 billion, while noting China has remained the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years and imported more than 90 trillion yuan ($13.4 trillion) worth of goods between 2021 and 2025. The piece emphasizes that investors judge markets by development prospects as well as size, so Xi's stress on innovation-driven growth was central; he urged deeper cooperation in science and technology, the digital economy and artificial intelligence alongside a green low-carbon transition. It describes China converting robots, autonomous driving and drone food delivery into momentum for high-quality development, and details Xi's pledge to accelerate building a modern industrial system by integrating scientific with industrial innovation, upgrading traditional industries, expanding emerging industries and planning future ones. The editorial also highlights commitments to reduce tariffs, expand market access, explore deeper reforms in rules administration and standards, fully implement both market access and operational access in manufacturing, and steadily expand openness in the services sector. It concludes that Xi's vision of an Asia-Pacific community prospering together offers an alternative to bloc politics, giving smaller and middle powers cooperation rather than pressure to choose sides, framing China's commitment as a durable economic policy grounded in open markets, technological exchange and peaceful coexistence.
items.title: Xi's APEC address framed as defense of openness amid rivalry

items.summary: CGTN's Tian Wei explores how China and the United States can pursue healthy competition while expanding cooperation to make artificial intelligence safer and its benefits more widely shared. As AI agents gain greater autonomy to make decisions and take actions, new risks are emerging, including systems escaping digital sandboxes and acting beyond authorized limits. The two countries are both described as AI powerhouses with distinct strengths: the United States is associated with frontier innovation from Silicon Valley, while China brings computing and energy infrastructure exemplified by Ulanqab. These complementary capabilities carry shared responsibilities for managing AI's risks and distributing its benefits.
items.title: China-US AI Cooperation and Safety Dialogue

items.summary:
A new study released Wednesday by the Pew Research Centre, reported through PTI from Washington on November 19, projects that Islam will surpass Christianity to become the world's largest religion by 2035. According to the projections, if current trends continue there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under three billion Christians worldwide by 2070. The study attributes most of this growth not to adult conversion but to births into each religious group. During 2020-2025, Pew reported a fertility rate for Muslims of 3.1 children per woman, compared with 2.5 for Christians and 1.6 for all other women, below the 2.1 replacement level needed for each generation to sustain itself.

The world's total population is projected to rise by 29 per cent between 2020 and 2070, with Christians growing by 30 per cent and Muslims by 80 per cent. Hindu numbers are expected to increase globally but decline slightly as a share of the global population: Hindus will grow from 15 per cent in 2020 to 14 per cent in 2070.

The absolute number of Hindus worldwide is projected to rise from 1.2 billion in 2020 to 1.4 billion by 2070, with India's Hindu population increasing by 176 million over the same period. Outside India, much of this growth will come from Pakistan (over five million) and the United States (over four million). Pew projects Hindus comprise 79.4 per cent of India's religious composition in 2020, sliding to 75.8 per cent by 2070, while Muslims rise from 15.2 per cent to 19.6 per cent over the same period even as India's overall fertility rate falls rapidly.

Nepal and India will remain the only two countries with a Hindu majority, and the United States is projected to have the world's fifth-largest Hindu population. Pakistan will hold the largest Muslim population globally, followed by India, Nigeria, and Indonesia, which currently has the most adherents to Islam. Buddhists are expected to shrink both in number and as a share of the global population, partly due to anticipated declines in China, South Korea, and Japan.

Regarding Christianity's geographic shift, more than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa by 2070, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo surpassing the United States as having the largest Christian population. The United States will no longer have a Christian majority, though Christians will remain its largest religious group.

The study also notes steady growth among "nones" -- people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated. Excluding China, which has high proportions of nones but faces sharp population decline, Pew projects the ranks of nones elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070. The nones already form a majority in ten countries including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Vietnam, with South Korea, France, and the United Kingdom forecast to join this group by 2070.
items.title: Pew projects Islam overtakes Christianity as world's largest religion by 2035

Stalin had not considered it, pointing out that the EWS quota was being implemented in central government employment, including in the railways, and urging the Chief Minister to take appropriate action.
items.title: Nagenthran Asserts Karthigai Deepam Will Be Lit at Thiruparankundram

The Nutrient Data Extraction API (formerly PSPDFKit) addresses errors where large language models present wrong document values as fact. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown, mapping fields from a document onto the user's JSON schema through split, classify and form endpoints that serve as building blocks for document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, receives a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient runs on its cloud API, self-hosted servers through an SDK or an Apple silicon Mac app.

The service offers four parse modes plus auto routing; when the mode is omitted it defaults to understand. Auto routes each page among structure, understand and agentic modes. Testing happens in Studio, a browser workspace for configuring parsing, extraction, classification, splitting and form filling on sample files before writing code. A typical loop uploads a document, drafts or generates a schema, runs it against fresh documents while inspecting values and citations, then saves the setup as a versioned preset called a processor with a proc_ ID; presets can be scored against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set.

On Nutrient's WholeDoc Bench parsing score of 86.2 on 5 November 2026 is not extraction accuracy, and extract adds $0.006 per page. The agentic setting tops the leaderboard at 86.2 for 1.8¢ per page versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting.

Grounded confidence combines optional signals of token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format; Nutrient's NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field, so each field also receives a match label of id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found, which should be gated on before confidence. When no score exists, confidence is omitted rather than low.

Pricing uses dollars from one balance shared across Nutrient's cloud APIs; the free plan gives $5 monthly covering about 330 understand-mode extractions, Starter costs $75 for $90 of usage and Growth costs $275 for $345. Understand-mode extraction runs at $15 per 1,000 pages while agentic parsing is $0.018 per page.

Nutrient's document decision model powers classify and split; the company reports a 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI's Jev. The hosted MCP server needs no API key, with Claude Code connecting in one command while Claude and Codex also work via OAuth.

Nutrient built and ran WholeDoc Bench across 480 documents, 30+ languages and seven areas; the code is Apache-2.0 with a 10-document public sample but the main test set remains private. Cross-page continuity is described as the biggest gap: on 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole, and charts remain hard at a best WholeDoc chart score of 64.5.

The demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks beyond the illustrative 0.97 confidence bar used for money fields in Nutrient's mortgage tutorial.
items.title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: Grounded JSON Parsing With Citations and Confidence
