The article reports that despite billions of dollars in government funding over recent years, North America has barely increased its ability to process heavy rare earths into defense-grade metals and magnets. MP Materials received more than $1 billion in combined financing, USA Rare Earth secured a $1.6 billion government financing package, and the Department of Defense and Department of Energy have funded pilot programs, feasibility studies, and demonstration projects across the sector. China still controls approximately 90% of global rare earth processing and produces nearly every ounce of dysprosium and terbium used in magnets powering American weapons systems.

On November 3, the U.S. Army signed a nonbinding term sheet with REalloys (Nasdaq: ALOY) to develop heavy rare earth processing at Tooele Army Depot in Utah. The deal covers approximately 200 acres, includes a potential 75-year lease and a right of first offer on production, and requires no government equity, taxpayer-funded construction, or grant money. REalloys will finance and build the facility while the Army provides land and security perimeter; REalloys pays fair-market rent and the Army receives participation rent once commercial operations begin.

Jeff Waksman, the Army's principal deputy assistant secretary for installations, energy and environment, said the arrangement lets the Army expand the critical minerals industrial base without putting taxpayer dollars at risk. The article notes that rare earth metallization is identified by the Center for Strategic and International Studies as the least developed and most difficult capability to rebuild outside China, requiring years of operational expertise rather than capital alone.

The Tooele model aligns incentives through a participation rent structure so REalloys must make economics work on its own. The Army would be first in line to purchase material before any other buyer but still has its own procurement process. In March 2026, the company won a Defense Logistics Agency contract to develop modular metallization technology for samarium and gadolinium.

The article states that REalloys' Euclid, Ohio facility holds an exclusive 80% offtake on production from the Saskatchewan Research Council's rare earth processing facility, which was designed without Chinese technology. The SRC facility targets annual capacity of approximately 525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide, and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide, with initial NdPr metallization capacity targeted for commissioning in Q1 2027.

In September 2026, REalloys appointed Dr. Muhammad Imran as Chief Operating Officer; the article states he is a former CTO of SRC with 17 years of rare earth processing experience and built the SRC processing technology. The company has secured feedstock agreements spanning Saskatchewan, Wyoming, Appalachia, Kazakhstan, Brazil, and Greenland, including a 15-year offtake for 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals' Tanbreez project.

The article states that at full scale REalloys envisions the largest heavy rare earth metallization facility in the Western world. On January 1, 2027, expanded Pentagon procurement rules take effect restricting Chinese-origin rare earth materials in American weapons systems; Beijing suspended its own export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements only until January 10, 2027.

The article states that REalloys is qualifying defense-grade materials ahead of the deadline with high-purity rare earth materials expected from SRC as early as Q4 2026. Evolution Metals & Technologies Corp. (Nasdaq: EMAT) is expanding its plant in Pohang, South Korea toward annual capacity above 10,000 metric tons; on October 31 the company raised fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to $10 million to $11 million while keeping a fiscal 2027 target of $400 million to $460 million.

The article states that Evolution's outlook is not based on contracted volumes and lists its ability to continue as a going concern among the risks. Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq: PPTA) received up to $40 million over 36 months from the Army's Defense Ordnance Technology Consortium for tungsten exploration at its Stibnite project in Idaho, matched by Perpetua with only about $18 million committed; on November 13 it reported $443.4 million in unrestricted cash while its $2.9 billion EXIM loan is not expected to close until the first quarter of 2027.

The article states that REalloys closed an approximately $100 million institutional private placement in June 2026 and reported $122.4 million in cash with virtually no debt; its leadership includes Chairman Stephen S. DuMont, President of GM Defense General Jack Keane (Ret.), and former Secretary of Defense Chief of Staff Joe Kasper.

Lithium Americas (NYSE: LAC) raised its Thacker Pass Phase 1 capital estimate to $3.83 billion from $2.93 billion on November 11, citing labor costs, added contingency, and tariffs; the article states it targets mechanical completion in late 2027.

Albemarle (NYSE: ALB) reported net sales of $1.55 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $646 million up 186% from a year earlier on November 4, with Energy Storage prices averaging $20.02 per kilogram of lithium carbonate equivalent; the article states it cut 2026 capital spending guidance to $300 million to $350 million from about $500 million.

The article concludes that if the Tooele model works, it could become a template where the federal government provides land, security, and demand while the private sector supplies capital, technology, and operational expertise. The publication is owned by Oilprice.com, which states it owns shares of REalloys and has an incentive to see its stock perform well; the article includes forward-looking statements with risks.
items.title: Army's nonbinding deal with REalloys for heavy rare earth processing at Tooele

items.summary: Union Minister G Kishan Reddy will pay the full Telangana SSC Board examination fees for 4,741 Class 10 students enrolled across 87 government schools within his Secunderabad Parliamentary Constituency. Described as a continuation of an initiative from previous years, the gesture is framed in keeping with the spirit of Antyodaya and aimed at encouraging students to pursue their education and build bright futures. The Minister extended best wishes to all examinees, urging them to approach the exams with confidence and determination. Separately, Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy emphasized that his government prioritizes the welfare of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs). During a meeting on Wednesday at the Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy Human Resource Development Institute in Telangana with Chairman Faggan Singh Kulaste and other members of the Parliamentary Committee on the Welfare of SCs and STs, Revanth Reddy briefed them that the government is creating opportunities for these communities across education, employment, economics, and politics. He highlighted political representation, including appointments as Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and state cabinet ministers, along with expanded roles in Public Service Commission positions and various state corporations. The Chief Minister also noted that SCs and STs receive priority wherever they meet necessary qualifications and merit, citing allocation of Indiramma housing scheme homes. This article was auto-generated from an agency feed and edited only for its headline by FPJ's editorial team.
items.title: Kishan Reddy to Cover SSC Fees for 4,741 Students in Secunderabad

items.summary: The Trump administration announced new measures this week that make it more difficult for Chinese companies to obtain some of the world's most advanced AI chips. For years, firms such as Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from overseas data centers, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally barred from physically importing into China through a practice known as remote access. Under plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers wishing to supply large amounts of computing power to China will now need special licenses and face additional regulatory burdens. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where officials suspect significant smuggling has occurred. These measures are not new policy ideas; similar proposals have circulated in Washington for some time. However, the timing of Monday's announcement coincides with a scandal involving Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence services and previously employed at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company linked to chip smuggling. A White House spokesperson told WIRED that the new rule would "crack down on the smuggling of advanced US chips" and help ensure America's most advanced chips go first to American innovators rather than Chinese shell companies. The restrictions trace their origins to fall 2022, when the Biden administration introduced rules designed to limit China's access to advanced AI chips and related manufacturing equipment. The strategy relied on restricting chip exports while American firms like Nvidia dominated the market for training hardware. Enforcement has fallen to the Bureau of Industry and Security within the Commerce Department, which had a budget of just $235 million in 2026. Megaspeed has become a prominent example of smuggling concerns at BIS, though it is not the only company suspected of involvement or necessarily the largest. According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of an estimated 136,000 AI chips that Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 were unaccounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips. Historically, Chinese companies did not need to physically import chips; they could rent overseas data center capacity without violating US export controls. Analysts had argued that allowing such access kept Chinese firms dependent on American technology and discouraged domestic alternatives, though restricting the practice would be difficult to enforce and could harm US chipmakers. Monday's announcement marks a shift toward regulating how Chinese companies use American technology even when hardware never enters China. Evidence suggests export controls have made it harder for Chinese AI companies to match their American competitors' computing power, but assessing the precise impact remains difficult. The restrictions have imposed costs on American suppliers: a Federal Reserve Bank of New York study estimated that earlier US export restrictions wiped $130 billion from affected companies' combined market value while hurting profitability and employment. China has responded by pursuing alternatives such as Huawei's megachip systems linking powerful chips together, and the DeepSeek lab demonstrated that improved training efficiency can yield competitive models with fewer resources.
items.title: Trump administration tightens controls on China's access to advanced AI chips

items.summary: During promotions for Netflix's series Akka, Keerthy Suresh and Radhika Apte appeared together. In an interview, Radhika discussed a Telugu film in which her character marries her maternal uncle (mama), stating she disliked everything about the movie. When asked by journalist Priyanka Nair, Keerthy explained that marrying one's maternal uncle is part of Tamil and Telugu culture. At a press conference for her upcoming film Sathyavan Savithiri, Keerthy responded to Radhika's remarks when journalists suggested South Indian cinema should address the situation. She said she had already spoken on the matter, noting at first she did not understand what Radhika meant before realizing it concerned culture. When told the practice is Tamil and Telugu rather than Malayalam, Keerthy corrected him, stating that this culture does not exist in Kerala and adding with respect that she would never let down their culture. She clarified that her earlier comments were offered as information. Netizens had speculated Radhika was referring to the 2014 film Legend, in which she starred opposite Nandamuri Balakrishna without naming it or its actor. NBK fans reacted negatively and resurfaced an older interview where Radhika expressed gratitude for being part of Legend. As of reporting, Radhika had not responded to the controversy. Sathyavan Savithiri, also starring Mysskin in the lead role, is scheduled to release on November 20, 2026.
items.title: Keerthy Suresh Defends South Indian Culture After Radhika Apte's Comments

items.summary: Nuclear recycling startup Project Omega has submitted a letter of intent to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, signaling its plan to file a full application within the next few years. The company is attempting to commercialize pyroprocessing technology that would recycle spent fuel into new reactor material while drastically reducing stored waste and hazard. CEO Staff Sheehan said nuclear waste is the industry's biggest challenge and Project Omega exists to reduce both the amount and danger of it. He noted that pyroprocessing cannot separate out pure plutonium, which he called a significant regulatory advantage over aqueous reprocessing used at facilities like La Hague in France or Mayak Production Association in Russia. The company emerged from stealth in February after Sheehan left Air Company, where he developed a process to convert carbon dioxide into hydrocarbons and alcohols for sustainable aviation fuel. Former NRC Chairman Chris Hanson joined as head of implementation. Project Omega has received Department of Energy funding at Idaho National Laboratory, military research with the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, and raised $80 million in a Series A round from Decisive Point venture firm last week. Sheehan said he would pitch his company identically to Democrats or Republicans because he is known as a climate advocate who sticks to his positions. The article also reported on several other stories: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang publicly called for his return as CEO after stepping down amid an extramarital affairs scandal, with the company reporting $116 billion in third quarter revenue; the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reassessed a permit for EDF Renewables' Atlantic Shores South offshore wind project despite Trump administration promises to ease renewables blockades; General Motors began searching for Mary Barra's successor among internal candidates including Paul Jacobson, Sterling Anderson, and Mark Reuss while developing its standalone battery business; Harvard researchers found grid-connected U.S. data center operations produced more greenhouse gas pollution from May 2024 to April 2025 than Denmark, though the study excluded diesel generators and behind-the-meter power plants; Quaise Energy signed a power purchase agreement with Google for 50 megawatts of electricity from its Project Obsidian superhot geothermal plant expected online by 2030 at about $350 million cost; North America's virtual power plant capacity grew nearly 26% this year to 47.2 gigawatts according to Wood Mackenzie analysis; and the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act faces amendments over National Historic Preservation Act changes affecting tribal sovereignty, with critics arguing the bill sidelines tribes through shorter consultation deadlines while proponents say it enshrines consultation in law.
items.title: Project Omega files NRC letter of intent for nuclear recycling license

items.summary: Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan returned to his residence in Rampur after being released from Dasna District Jail in Ghaziabad on interim bail. The Allahabad High Court granted the relief on Tuesday, observing that the mandatory provisions governing his arrest were prima facie not strictly followed. He addressed the media Wednesday evening and thanked the court for granting him relief, saying his release was a day of celebration for those who believe in constitutional values, justice, and democracy. Khan said he firmly believed the country is independent but the Constitution is not, adding that people must demand the Constitution be freed. Speaking on the political situation, he declared "Chunav nahi hoga, Inquilab hoga" (no elections will happen, revolution will), asserting contests would now be based on issues rather than caste or religion. He defended himself against mafia allegations, noting he opened schools for children and established a university, and questioned why investigating agencies like the ED, CBI, I-T, and Development Authority did not jail educationists such as Madan Mohan Malaviya and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan if they existed in their time. Targeting the BJP, Khan alleged it had suffered election setbacks and claimed its won seats were secured through foul play, citing both Lok Sabha and Vidhan Parishad results. His son Abdullah Azam Khan arrived at Dasna Jail to welcome him along with SP supporters. The money laundering case relates to Mohammad Ali Jauhar University, a private university in Rampur founded by Azam Khan in 2006; on October 28 the ED attached its land and building, putting the book value of the property at Rs 426 crore while its estimated current market value was Rs 1,170 crore. The article is directly published from ANI without editing by DNA staff.
items.title: Azam Khan Granted Interim Bail in ED Case

items.summary: Severe Cyclonic Storm 'Akvan' is developing over the westcentral Bay of Bengal, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) assessing it as likely to move north-northwestwards and cross the North Andhra Pradesh-Yanam and South Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri by noon on Thursday. The IMD estimates maximum sustained wind speeds of 90-100 kmph, gusting to 110 kmph, with landfall expected on November 20 in that same stretch from Narsapur to Puri. In response, the Odisha government has mandated closure of all government, aided and private schools along with Anganwadi centres across six districts for three days, running from November 19 to November 21. Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi stated at a review meeting held in the State Control Room that the state was fully prepared and had begun taking necessary measures. He noted that heavy rainfall is expected across several Odisha districts, with wind speeds averaging around 100 kmph, particularly affecting southern Odisha and the coastal belt extending as far as Balasore—including Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, and Kalahandi—and reported that a Red Warning has been issued for 13 districts. The state government reportedly held discussions with District Collectors on comprehensive management and response strategy. In parallel, Railway authorities rescheduled three trains due to the cyclone: Train No. 18046 Charlapalli-Shalimar East Coast Express was moved from a 08:40 departure at 15:40 hours on November 19; Train No. 12704 Secunderabad-Howrah Falaknuma Express shifted its departure to 17:55 hours, up from 15:55 hours the same day; and Train No. 15227 SMVT Bengaluru-Muzaffarpur Express moved from a 00:30 departure to 08:30 hours on Thursday. The Indian Navy and other agencies are coordinating preparedness measures while authorities monitor the cyclone's movement, though IMD figures represent forecasts rather than confirmed conditions.
items.title: Cyclone Akvan Reshapes Coastal India with School Closures and Train Reschedules

items.summary:
The UK faces an emerging risk to gas security, according to a fresh update from the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which says that the danger of insufficient gas during a cold snap remains and calls for an enduring solution. Neso's report stated: "Our updated analysis shows that the risk identified in our 2025 assessment remains, and that there is an ongoing need for an enduring solution to secure future gas supply." Even with new North Sea production such as Jackdaw flowing into the national network this week, the UK will still depend on imports. Possible remedies include additional import terminals, interconnecting pipes to the continent, or reliable domestic gas storage, possibly in combination.

On the storage front, events are moving faster than government decision-making. Centrica has not been filling Rough, the largest offshore storage facility, and will close it next spring unless a deal is reached with the government. Meanwhile, fellow FTSE 100 firm SSE says it is preparing to begin closing its Atwick facility near Hornsea in East Yorkshire, which represents about 20% of Great Britain's onshore gas storage. Both firms are acting rationally from a commercial standpoint: the economics of gas storage depend on summer prices being reliably lower than winter ones to secure a profit margin. In an increasingly global liquefied natural gas market those spreads have disappeared, and geopolitical factors such as the closure of the strait of Hormuz can further complicate matters.

While Atwick could probably be reopened after closure, that is less true of Rough. The government's position has not moved since summer, when it conceded for the first time that intervention may be necessary. An energy department statement repeated: "We recently confirmed plans to explore commercial support for storage and the wider sector, to help protect our gas security." It added that proposals would be set out in due course.

The article argues this is leaving things late. Belt-and-braces gas security for winter already required an eleventh-hour deal with Belgium to avert a planned cut in interconnector capacity. Delay has reportedly handed negotiating clout to the operators if ministers ultimately need to strike a deal, and the storage question cannot wait much longer.

The article notes that the security problem has been recognised for years, even before the first Neso report, yet successive governments have taken remarkably long to assemble a strategy while urging households to stockpile gas. It concludes that it is time for a plan before further facilities close and narrow options.
items.title: UK Gas Storage at Risk as Facilities Close Amid Delayed Government Plan

items.summary: On Wednesday, Alexander Rossnagel, data protection commissioner for Hesse, announced that his office has opened an investigation into Deutsche Bank following a massive leak of more than 15 million internal records. The probe concerns possible violations of data protection law and will examine whether the bank had adequate protective measures in place and whether it reported the breach to affected individuals promptly, according to Rossnagel's statement: "I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals." The leak was carried out by whistleblowers who shared internal documents with a group of international media outlets. Those documents reportedly revealed that the bank had ignored repeated internal warnings about money laundering, corruption and sanctions violations, and named clients including Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump, and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In response to the revelations, Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing acknowledged mistakes in an interview with Handelsblatt, stating: "When you look at the events today, you naturally question whether something could have been done differently." He added that reviewing past decisions might reveal points where priorities could have shifted, while denying that he sought to overlook risks and explaining his reasoning for streamlining customer review processes. The bank said it had reinforced its controls after these matters "date back many years," but the leak has damaged its reputation and pushed its share price down. Deutsche Bank maintains that it proactively informed the relevant authorities about the breach, claims testing found no access to account information, login credentials or payment data, and noted that although the probe will not examine the leaked documents themselves, it will assess the technical and organisational measures in place to determine whether they were appropriate.
items.title: German regulator probes Deutsche Bank over 15 million-file leak

items.summary: On Wednesday, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela during an unexpected visit to Caracas, according to state television reporting. He was received by interim leader Delcy Rodríguez ahead of a planned trip to Colombia later that same day, where he intends to discuss bilateral security cooperation. Framing the deal as a renewal of defence partnership and an opportunity for the two nations' armed forces to work together, Hegseth's remarks were broadcast via footage from VTV, Venezuela's state television channel. The visit had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon beforehand. This move represents another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas that followed Nicolás Maduro's capture in January. The agreement resumes technical and military cooperation between the two countries after years of suspension amid deteriorating diplomatic relations. Rodríguez stated that a primary objective is strengthening Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training programmes, which she said would improve preparedness to respond to shared threats. The deal also aims to enhance operational equipment for Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. Neither government has yet disclosed details on the implementation timeline, resources involved, or specific mechanisms of cooperation. Rodríguez assumed power after Maduro's capture, though her continued leadership remains uncertain as her interim mandate expired in July with no announced date for the next presidential election. The broader Washington-Caracas rapprochement has also included agreements over Venezuelan oil and a US strategy against drug trafficking in the Caribbean and Pacific, which has caused at least 240 deaths since September 2025 in attacks on vessels suspected of carrying drugs. Hegseth's visit is part of efforts by Donald Trump's administration to expand its influence in Venezuela; he was the third member of Trump's cabinet to travel there this year, following trips by the interior and energy secretaries focused on Venezuela's oil and mineral resources.
items.title: US Defence Secretary Announces Military Cooperation with Venezuela in Surprise Caracas Visit

items.summary: Prof Caroline Mitchell of Keele University, writing as a GP in Sheffield, argues that software built for the fragmented US insurance-based system does not fit the universal public service model of the NHS. She notes that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature within the UK context because they were developed primarily for an entirely different healthcare environment. To illustrate this mismatch, she cites a consultant who described managing seven bolt-on software systems across a single consultation, one focused on billing functions, and contrasts it with a senior US hospital administrator's view that most American health data systems exist mainly to record care for reimbursement. She emphasizes that NHS general practice records are designed to support lifelong patient care and safe prescribing rather than tracking insurance allowances consumed during the year, pointing out how astounded her colleague was by this difference in purpose. Mitchell also questions why the NHS should rely on a US firm to manage its data when the UK has demonstrated healthcare-software innovation of its own, specifically citing Emis, developed with GP leadership, which transformed primary care IT decades ago. She concludes that software built for an insurance market may simply not be the best fit for universal healthcare systems.
items.title: Letter arguing Palantir is ill-suited to NHS healthcare

items.summary: On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a stop in Caracas to announce an agreement deepening defense cooperation with Venezuela. The visit followed the U.S. military operation 10 months earlier that bombed Venezuelan territory and removed Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores from power before transferring them to prison in New York. Hegseth, who will travel to Colombia later Wednesday before continuing on to Ecuador, framed the agreement as ensuring Venezuelans are not threatened by foreign actors, narco-terrorists, or criminals. He delivered remarks from a standing microphone beside acting President Delcy Rodríguez, saying both nations look forward to unlocking Venezuela's prosperity and stability for a safer hemisphere and America. Hegseth noted that Venezuela could draw on U.S. military experience to strengthen security within its sovereign borders. The visit came with little advance notice and limited media presence after Hegseth stopped at U.S. Southern Command headquarters in Doral, Florida. Rodríguez received him hours after returning from a Middle East tour of Turkey, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. She was accompanied by Defense Minister Gustavo González López, Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, and businessman Alejandro Betancourt of NABEP, described as a key figure in oil agreements Venezuela has signed with the United States through a Pentagon office. Military and counternarcotics cooperation between Caracas and Washington had been severed in 2005 during Hugo Chávez's presidency. Chávez ended a relationship that included military technology sharing and joint defense exercises, after which Venezuela turned to Russia, Iran, and China as its main suppliers of military equipment. Hegseth is the highest-ranking Pentagon official to visit Venezuela since the operation removed Maduro from power earlier this year, though several senior Defense Department officials have already made repeated trips. These include General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who commanded Operation Absolute Resolution on January 3; Southern Command chief Francis Donovan, who oversaw warship and aircraft deployments off the Venezuelan coast as well as strikes against boats allegedly carrying narcotics before U.S. personnel entered Venezuelan territory; Deputy Undersecretary Joseph Humire, who visited in February; and CIA Director John Ratcliffe. The cooperation being formalized has not been limited to official visits but has been underway for months. At least two military and law-enforcement operations carried out in Venezuela over the past year were supported by the United States through equipment and intelligence-sharing. In June, authorities launched an operation against the hideout of Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, known as Niño Guerrero, leader of the Tren de Aragua criminal organization designated a terrorist group by Washington, in the gold-mining region of southern Bolívar State. More recently, drones were used to destroy an operations center belonging to the National Liberation Army guerrilla group in Apure State. In both cases, questions remain about the number and identities of those killed.
items.title: Hegseth Announces U.S.-Venezuela Defense Cooperation Agreement

items.summary: A reliability watchdog reports that the North American power grid is less at risk of winter blackouts than it was this time last year. The North American Electric Reliability Corp., or NERC, found only three areas are now in an elevated risk category during cold snaps, down from seven a year ago, because there would not be enough reserved capacity to meet peak demand. NERC attributed the improvement to more than 26 gigawatts of new winter peak capacity, driven by about nine gigawatts each of battery storage and gas generation. California and Texas led in deploying storage, while Texas, northern Mexico, and the Mountain West accounted for the largest gas expansions. Emergency orders from the Department of Energy are also helping shore up the grid: they allow operators to direct data centers and other large facilities onto backup generators during peak demand even if it means breaching air pollution limits, and they keep six fossil fuel plants online past their scheduled retirement dates despite raising costs for customers and greenhouse gas emissions. In the United States, only North and South Carolina remain in the elevated risk category amid rapid growth in residential electric heating plus large data centers and industrial loads, which has steadily eroded reserve margins especially during early morning hours before solar generation ramps up. Canadian provinces including Quebec and Nova Scotia are also at elevated risk mainly because gas pipelines are constrained. The assessment arrives as Americans grow concerned about grid reliability; outages are getting longer due to more extreme weather from rising global temperatures, while utilities struggle to modernize fast enough for demand from data centers, reshored manufacturing, and a more electrified economy. Recent nationwide blackout fears spread across social media stemmed from a false manipulated clip of President Donald Trump shared by an account pushing cryptocurrency, per Politifact, with additional anxiety fueled by technology failures affecting air travel, banks, Microsoft, and Apple. Beyond reliability, NERC oversees cybersecurity threats to the bulk power system through mandatory standards for utilities and grid operators aimed at preventing cyber and physical attacks on electric, natural gas, and transmission infrastructure, and serves as the primary hub for sharing sensitive incident data, attack indicators, and vulnerability alerts. In January, NERC said these controls remain critical but are not being updated fast enough to keep pace with changing threats; a major fix would require employees or third-party vendors connecting remotely to smaller energy sites to use two-step login verifications, covering solar, wind, and battery projects as well as substations and fossil fuel plants. Two-step verification is already required of the largest power plants, transmission hubs, and regional control centers. It typically takes several years before updated NERC standards are approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and enforced, and NERC did not reply to a request for comment by publication time.
items.title: North American grid faces fewer winter blackouts, but risks and cyber gaps persist

items.summary: Following a May 2026 government overhaul of private renting that abolished no-fault evictions and moved tenancies onto rolling contracts, the government has acknowledged that deposit protection remains unresolved for many tenants. While reforms are promised and consulting is underway on scrapping insured deposit schemes, the timing of these changes has not yet been confirmed. Housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook said landlords and letting agents remain permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts, creating a power imbalance. The government is now seeking firsthand accounts from private tenants about their experiences with the rental deposit system in England, asking whether they struggled to recover their deposit, whether it was withheld or subject to deductions for damage, and how long disputes took to resolve.
items.title: England private renters invited to report deposit protection struggles

items.summary: After a quiet period following his 2008 departure from EA and Maxis, Will Wright is promoting his next project, MyMems, which uses generative AI to build a game-like experience from players' memories. The title is slated for release next year and comes from Wright's Gallium Studios in partnership with Artificial Agency. According to the studio's press release, MyMems differentiates itself by 'turn[ing] the simulation inward,' mining player-provided memories to create digital people who form teams to solve puzzles within the game world. Wright illustrates this concept with examples such as imagining a Grand Slam match between his grandmother and Serena Williams, or selecting three real-life contacts to help build a bridge across a chasm. He noted that The Sims' 'plausible behavior' failed to capture real-life nuances like claustrophobia or family conflict, prompting the shift toward personalizing games using actual memories and experiences of people players know. Wright said MyMems will extract generalized themes from memories into self-contained zones he compared to theme park areas, with sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths each potentially forming their own playable sections. Players can also create worlds based on shared memories involving family, friends, and co-workers.
items.title: Will Wright's AI memory-based simulation MyMems

items.summary: Ukrainian authorities, working with the FBI, arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware organization linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies worldwide. The arrests followed a two-year investigation into a cybercrime group comprising at least 27 individuals from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries, which was connected to a larger network of more than 60 members across eight jurisdictions that included former Conti gang members. According to acting National Police chief Maksym Tsutskiridze speaking with Censor.NET, the organization targeted companies in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, and financial sectors as well as critical infrastructure. Investigators said attackers researched victims' finances, assets, employees, and IT vulnerabilities before launching attacks designed to steal data, encrypt systems, and extort cryptocurrency payments. Tsutskiridze stated that at least 28 companies transferred more than $40.5 million in ransoms, equivalent to approximately UAH 1.8 billion, noting this was money already paid while the full extent of damage remained under assessment. Court records identify Warren Oil Company as a victim of an August 2024 attack in which hackers copied 1.4 TB of data before receiving an 84.5 BTC ransom payment equivalent to approximately $5 million at the time, and describe how attackers initially demanded $10 million but ultimately received $5 million after negotiations. Records also allege Newpark Resources paid $1.5 million in December 2024 while Quantum Health paid $5 million in June 2026 following an initial $15 million ransom demand. LeMagIT reported that the BlackSuit gang claimed Maxxis International as a victim in November 2024, and Ukrainian court records identify Chaos as the ransomware used by the organization. The Conti operation shut down in May 2022 with members dispersing into smaller gangs including BlackSuit, which operated first as Quantum ransomware before becoming Royal and then BlackSuit after high-profile attacks such as one against Dallas, Texas. However, Ukrainian authorities have not identified the four arrested suspects as former Conti members or confirmed their individual affiliations with BlackSuit or Chaos. To breach corporate networks, attackers impersonated IT support personnel using a custom platform with AI-generated voice messages to automate fraudulent calls that tricked employees into disclosing login credentials or installing remote-access software; in one incident an attacker kept an employee on the phone while another accessed systems until intrusion was confirmed. Court records describe additional tactics including phishing pages impersonating corporate VPN services, spoofed phone numbers, and tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk, with attackers obtaining two-factor authentication codes to gain network access during the Warren Oil attack before stealing information and encrypting files. Tsutskiridze explained that victims were pressured from both sides by data encryption and threats to publish stolen information, forcing cryptocurrency ransom payments. Ukrainian authorities conducted 66 simultaneous searches across Kyiv and 11 regions of Ukraine as part of the joint operation with U.S. law enforcement; four suspected key members were detained though their exact arrest locations were not disclosed. During these searches investigators seized computers, mobile phones, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash, and €20,000. The suspects face charges related to participating in a criminal organization and unauthorized interference with information systems under Ukrainian law, carrying up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Authorities say the investigation is ongoing as they work to identify additional members of the international network and their involvement in other cyberattacks, while also releasing investigative video footage including raids, seized cash, interviews, suspect questioning, and audio from an alleged extortion call demanding $15 million after claiming to have stolen more than 1.5 TB of corporate data.
items.title: Ukraine and FBI Arrest Ransomware Gang Members Linked to $40M in Ransoms

items.summary: Equinor, Europe's largest pipeline gas supplier, is battling an ongoing cyberattack on its IT systems while European gas prices remain nearly triple last year's level amid the Hormuz crisis. The FBI warned that state-aligned hackers and criminals are using AI-powered tools to breach corporate networks in under three hours. Attacks on energy companies have risen across every measure since 2024, with Check Point recording nearly 70% more attacks on U.S. utilities in the first eight months of 2024 than the same period in 2023, and by May that year U.S. energy firms were fielding about 1,755 attacks a week each. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups targeting industrial companies in 2025, up from 80 the prior year. Equinor stated on Wednesday it now understands how the attack was carried out and which systems were hit, noting that the attack is not a virus and cannot spread, with no data theft found and no effect on oil and gas output, though restoration timelines remain uncertain. Norway's National Security Authority raised its cyber threat level to the second-highest tier in October after pro-Russian hackers took control of a hydropower dam at Lake Risevatnet in western Norway in April 2025, opening a valve for four hours. Eight months later, Russian state-linked hackers struck Poland's energy system on December 29, 2025, hitting more than 30 wind and solar farms plus a large combined heat-and-power plant, damaging remote terminal units, protection relays and communications equipment; CERT Polska attributed it to the group Berserk Bear while ESET and Dragos linked it to Sandworm. In December 2025, 26 Western security agencies warned that Cyber Army of Russia Reborn, NoName057(16), Z-Pentest and Sector16 had breached poorly secured industrial equipment in energy, water and food sectors across the West; the U.S. Justice Department says the Kremlin funded Cyber Army of Russia Reborn's DDoS-for-hire subscriptions, and Sector16 member Artem Revenskii agreed to plead guilty in California over attacks on oil and gas infrastructure in the United States, Ukraine, Germany, France and Latvia after investigators found messages discussing deforming pipelines. Since April, Iranian state hackers have targeted internet-connected controllers made by Rockwell, Siemens and Schneider Electric at U.S. water and energy providers, with one provider's controller logic rewritten to disable shutdown and alarm functions; suspected Iran-linked hackers also breached tank gauges at gas stations in several states, altering fuel readings per CNN, and were suspected in a four-day British power plant shutdown in July. Iran works through criminal hackers as well: the group Pioneer Kitten handed network access to ransomware gangs for a share of ransoms, with Pay2Key raising affiliates' shares from 70% to 80% for attacks on the United States and Israel, described by KELA as Iran outsourcing geopolitical retribution. Criminal groups have also targeted energy firms for profit: Qilin claimed nearly a terabyte of data from Romania's oil pipeline operator Conpet in February without affecting transport, Gentlemen encrypted systems at Oltenia Energy Complex in December 2025, and TrendAI researchers found a German renewable firm's internal database listed for about $748,000 on criminal forums. The IMF warned that AI is making cyberattacks cheaper, faster and more dangerous; the FBI said ARTEX has been used since at least August against energy and nine other sectors, while Google reported hackers using AI agents to find flaws, write exploits and launch them without human involvement for the first time observed in August, when attackers also used AI-generated scripts targeting Siemens controllers. The damage so far relies on old weaknesses: weak or default passwords accounted for 26% of Dragos' findings at oil and gas companies last year, internet-facing systems for another 26%, and poor separation between business and control networks for 29%. Brian Proctor noted that the barrier once requiring expertise is now time, which is shrinking. Equinor remains working with Norway's national security authorities to contain an attack whose source it has not named.
items.title: Equinor Cyberattack Amid Rising Energy Sector Threats

items.summary: BJP ally Sanjay Nishad, Uttar Pradesh Cabinet Minister and chief of the Nishad Party, staged a sit-in in Maharajganj demanding Scheduled Caste (SC) status for the Nishad-Mallah community. The protest unfolded with his supporters after he was attending an event with party workers; he urged them to take to the streets because their reservation demand would not be met without public demonstration. He then led his followers onto the road and sat down in protest, converting the gathering into a demonstration over inclusion in the Scheduled Caste category. Nishad said the sit-in would continue until BJP's Uttar Pradesh president Pankaj Chaudhary secured an assurance from Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the demand. He chose Maharajganj because it is Chaudhary's Lok Sabha constituency, and he argued that the BJP state president's proximity to the Prime Minister makes him well placed to raise the issue directly with Modi before any withdrawal of the protest could be considered. The demonstration occurred even though the Nishad Party remains an ally of the BJP in Uttar Pradesh, where Nishad serves as a Cabinet minister in the Yogi Adityanath government.
items.title: Nishad Party chief protests for SC status

On Monday night, Ukraine launched back-to-back drone and cruise missile strikes on the Kerch Strait Bridge that links annexed Crimea to Russia's mainland. The first wave left one of the bridge's twin arches slumping sideways; the second brought that arch and a stretch of highway crashing into the sea below. The rail section running parallel to the road remains operational, though passengers captured footage showing a gap where the roadway once stood, with tangled concrete and reinforced steel now lying in the water beneath a shipping route between Russia's Sea of Azov and Black Sea holdings.

The attack was described as the fourth against the bridge since 2022. In October 2022, a truck bomb killed five people including the driver and brought several spans down. In July 2023, Ukrainian naval drones struck it, killing a Russian family visiting from Belgorod. In June 2025, Ukraine said it had launched an underwater attack on the bridge's supports; Russia claimed no damage.

President Volodymyr Zelensky framed the strikes as the final step of a seven-stage operation that gradually degraded Russian radar, air defence and electronic jamming to expose the bridge. He announced the attacks via social media with the message "War will always return to where it began," timed for Wednesday's three-way meeting between Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Natia Seskuria of the Royal United Services Institute noted that Moscow has long used the bridge to move personnel, fuel, equipment and ammunition into southern Ukraine. However, after Russian forces seized a land corridor linking Crimea to Russia's Rostov region at the mouth of the Don River, dependence on the bridge declined though it was not eliminated. Seskuria said the damage reduces flexibility by removing one route for redistributing traffic but does not cut off Crimea or sever supply lines.

The bridge remains important as an everyday transport link connecting Crimean residents with Russia; over summer fuel restrictions were imposed amid strikes on oil depots, tankers and transport facilities. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov downplayed the attacks, saying "There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored - and will be even better than it was before."
items.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Strait Bridge, damaging road section

Indian budget airline SpiceJet has received board approval to raise up to ₹5,500 crore as it faces financial and operational difficulties. During a Wednesday meeting, the board approved the fundraising proposal and informed potential investors of ongoing discussions. If successful, the funds would be raised through a combination of equity and other permitted instruments, strengthening the airline's balance sheet while supporting its revival. The board has directed management to complete all necessary processes at the earliest.

The company also reportedly approved increasing its authorised share capital from ₹2,000 crore to ₹7,500 crore, though this requires shareholder and regulatory approval. SpiceJet plans to deploy the funds toward fleet expansion, meeting operational requirements, and rebuilding its network. Chairman and Managing Director Ajay Singh said the fundraising would provide an important opportunity to rebuild the airline and restore its brand.

The airline is operating in a difficult environment shaped by geopolitical tensions and airspace restrictions affecting nearly all operations, alongside steep increases in aviation turbine fuel prices that have added pressure on costs. SpiceJet has also been losing ground in India's domestic market: according to DGCA data, its domestic share fell from 1.2% in August to 0.6% in September 2026. The airline continues to struggle with unpaid dues, operational fleet and crew shortages, plus widespread cancellations and delays.

Shares gained 4.95% on Wednesday, closing at ₹9.97 on the BSE after the announcement of the proposed fundraising.
items.title: SpiceJet board approves ₹5,500 crore fundraising amid crisis

The Board of Peace, chaired by President Donald Trump and established under his administration, issued its second report to the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday. The board warned that the fragile Gaza peace deal could collapse if Israel and Hamas fail to recommit to pledges made during negotiations. According to a Bloomberg News review of the document, first reported by the Associated Press, the board stated the Gaza peace process cannot advance until an International Stabilization Force deploys in the enclave, Israel fulfills its commitments, and Iran-backed Hamas militants surrender their weapons. The report quoted the board as saying that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” adding that if it collapses there would be no Roadmap to return to, no administration to deploy, and no enabling environment to rebuild.

The assessment follows months of intermittent clashes, Israeli airstrikes, and a deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza. The board described progress as “limited” and “imperfect,” noting the Palestinian population faces another winter living in tents and rubble. It called on Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, urged both parties to demilitarize, and requested greater UN support.

The report comes a year after the Security Council approved Trump's Gaza plan, though many steps from that original agreement remain unmet: the Palestinian committee meant to govern Gaza has not entered the territory, and an international security force intended to police Gaza and oversee its demilitarization has not deployed. The UN said on Tuesday that already dire living conditions for Palestinians were worsening amid winter flooding.

Violence continued during this period; the UN human rights office reported Israeli strikes had killed more than 1,600 Palestinians since the ceasefire was announced, citing Gaza health ministry data. Funding also remained insufficient, with the UN humanitarian aid appeal only about 40% funded. The board noted that Israeli restrictions on supplies and equipment into Gaza hampered winter preparations, though Israel cited concerns over Hamas diverting dual-use items for military purposes as its reason for limiting critical materials.
items.title: Trump's Board of Peace Warns Gaza Ceasefire Could Collapse
